articles.title: Claude Code Custom System Prompts in 2026: Overriding Defaults, Appending Instructions, and What You Cannot Change
articles.description: Developers discover that Claude Code ignores custom instructions because they set them in the wrong layer. Learn the three ways to shape Claude Code behavior, what the system prompt actually controls, and which parts remain locked no matter what you
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Custom System Prompts in 2026: Overriding Defaults, Appending Instructions, and What You Cannot Change

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers add custom instructions to Claude Code, restart the session, and watch Claude ignore them. The instructions sit in a CLAUDE.md file, or a settings.json key, or an --append-system-prompt flag, but Claude still responds with the default behavior. This confusion stems from a misunderstanding of where each layer applies and what the system prompt actually controls.

Claude Code provides three distinct mechanisms for shaping behavior: replacing or appending to the system prompt with CLI flags, defining persistent project context in CLAUDE.md files, and configuring output styles that transform how Claude formats responses. Each mechanism operates at a different layer of the request cycle, and mixing them without understanding their boundaries produces configuration that appears broken but is working exactly as designed.

The system prompt itself is not a single editable file. Claude Code builds it from multiple sources at request time, and certain parts remain locked regardless of configuration. Understanding which parts you can change, which require a different mechanism, and which remain fixed is the difference between instructions that work and instructions that vanish.

This post examines the three ways to customize Claude Code behavior, explains what each mechanism controls, and clarifies which built-in behaviors cannot be changed no matter which layer you modify.

Key Takeaways

  • Claude Code builds the system prompt from multiple sources; replacing or appending text with CLI flags changes the core identity and tool guidance, while CLAUDE.md injects project context into the conversation separately.
  • The --system-prompt flag replaces the entire default prompt including tool descriptions and safety instructions, while --append-system-prompt preserves the default and adds extra rules on top.
  • CLAUDE.md files do not modify the system prompt; they inject content into the conversation as project context that Claude reads alongside the system prompt.
  • Output styles, skills, and permission rules shape behavior through separate mechanisms that remain active regardless of system prompt customization.
  • Built-in safety instructions, tool definitions, and API-level constraints cannot be overridden through any system prompt flag or configuration file.

Understanding System Prompt Presets: claude_code vs Custom Strings

Claude Code does not expose the full default system prompt as an editable file. The official documentation confirms this: "Claude Code's system prompt isn't published. To give Claude standing instructions, use CLAUDE.md files or the --append-system-prompt flag." Developers who expect a single text file controlling Claude's identity will not find one, because the prompt assembles from multiple internal sources at runtime.

The default prompt includes the following components:

  • Core identity and role definition
  • Tool descriptions and usage guidance for each available capability
  • Safety and security instructions
  • Coding conventions and best practices
  • Output formatting rules

When developers pass --system-prompt or --system-prompt-file, they replace all of these components with their own text. Claude Code discards the default identity, tool guidance, and safety instructions, leaving the developer responsible for defining everything from scratch.

This replacement makes sense for non-coding agents where Claude Code's default identity does not fit the task, but it creates problems when developers simply want to add domain-specific rules without rebuilding the entire prompt. For that use case, --append-system-prompt preserves the default and adds extra instructions after it.

The choice between replacement and append determines whether developers inherit Claude Code's built-in tool guidance. A replaced prompt loses descriptions of how the Bash tool works, when to use Read versus Write, and which permission checks apply before tool execution. An appended prompt keeps those descriptions and layers new instructions on top.

Appending Instructions: Extending the Default Without Starting From Scratch

The --append-system-prompt and --append-system-prompt-file flags let developers extend the default prompt without replacing it. This preserves Claude Code's identity as a coding assistant while adding project-specific conventions, output requirements, or domain context.

A typical use case: enforcing a consistent code review format. Developers want Claude to check for specific patterns in every review without changing how Claude uses tools or responds to questions. Appending instructions achieves this:

// Start Claude Code with custom review rules appended
// Shell command:
// claude --append-system-prompt-file ./review-rules.txt

// Contents of review-rules.txt:
When reviewing code, always check for:
1. Missing error handling in async functions
2. Hardcoded configuration values that should be environment variables
3. Console.log statements that should be removed before production
4. Tests that need updating after implementation changes

Format your review as:
- Summary (2-3 sentences)
- Findings (bulleted list with file:line references)
- Risk level (low/medium/high)

Claude receives the default system prompt followed by a blank line and then the appended text. The blank line separates the default instructions from the custom rules, making the boundary clear when debugging what Claude sees.

Developers can combine both inline text and file contents by passing both --append-system-prompt and --append-system-prompt-file in the same command (requires Claude Code v2.1.283 or later). The file contents appear first, followed by a blank line, then the inline text:

// Combine file and inline instructions
// Shell command:
// claude --append-system-prompt-file ./style.md --append-system-prompt "Always reply in French"

// Claude receives:
// 1. Default system prompt
// 2. Blank line
// 3. Contents of style.md
// 4. Blank line
// 5. "Always reply in French"

This ordering ensures that persistent style rules from the file remain stable across runs while allowing per-invocation overrides through the inline flag.

Claude Code system prompt layers

The appended text applies to a single session. Starting a new session without the flags returns to the default prompt. Developers who need persistent instructions that apply across all sessions should use CLAUDE.md files instead, which inject content at a different layer.

CLAUDE.md vs System Prompts: What Actually Goes Where

CLAUDE.md files do not modify the system prompt. This distinction trips up developers who expect CLAUDE.md to work like a persistent --append-system-prompt, but CLAUDE.md operates through a separate mechanism that injects content into the conversation as project context.

The Agent SDK documentation states: "CLAUDE.md takes a different path: the SDK reads it and injects its content into the conversation as project context, so it shapes behavior alongside whichever system prompt you choose." This injection happens after the system prompt is built, meaning CLAUDE.md cannot override tool guidance or safety instructions that live in the system prompt layer.

Aspect System Prompt Flags CLAUDE.md Files
Scope Single session Persistent across sessions
Timing Applied at prompt assembly Injected into conversation
Can override tool guidance Yes (with --system-prompt) No
Can define project conventions Yes (with --append) Yes
Requires restart after edit No (takes effect immediately) No (watched for changes)
Location CLI flag Project .claude/ directory

CLAUDE.md excels at defining what the project is, what conventions it follows, and what context Claude needs to understand it. System prompt flags excel at defining who Claude is and how Claude should respond. When developers put project conventions in the system prompt or try to redefine Claude's identity in CLAUDE.md, the configuration fights against the mechanism's design.

A well-structured setup uses CLAUDE.md for project facts:

// .claude/CLAUDE.md contents:
# Project: TypeScript API Server

This project uses:
- Express 4.18 with TypeScript 5.3
- Jest for testing with 80%+ coverage requirement
- Zod for runtime validation
- Prisma 5.x for database access

Conventions:
- All API routes live in src/routes/
- Database models use singular names (User, not Users)
- Environment variables are required at startup (fail fast)
- Error responses follow RFC 7807 Problem Details format

And system prompt flags for response requirements:

// Pass this flag when starting Claude Code:
// --append-system-prompt "When suggesting code changes, always include the full file path and a brief explanation of why the change is needed"

This separation lets developers change project facts without touching how Claude formats responses, and change response formatting without modifying project documentation.

What You Cannot Override: Built-In Safety, Tool Definitions, and Hard Limits

Certain parts of Claude Code behavior remain fixed regardless of system prompt configuration. These restrictions protect against unsafe operations, ensure consistent tool behavior, and enforce API-level constraints that no client-side configuration can bypass.

Three categories of behavior cannot be overridden:

Safety and security instructions. Claude Code includes built-in rules that prevent certain operations even when the system prompt requests them. These rules operate at a layer below the system prompt, meaning a custom --system-prompt text cannot remove them. Examples include refusal to generate malware, restrictions on processing sensitive data without explicit permission, and guardrails against executing commands that could compromise the system.

Tool definitions and behavior. The tools Claude Code exposes (Bash, Read, Write, Edit, and others) have fixed definitions that describe their parameters, when to use them, and what they return. A custom system prompt can provide additional guidance on tool usage, but it cannot change the tool's signature or disable built-in tool restrictions. For instance, developers cannot use --system-prompt to make the Read tool bypass permission checks or force the Bash tool to run commands without approval when project settings require it.

API and model constraints. Token limits, rate limits, and model capabilities are set by the Anthropic API and cannot be increased through configuration. A system prompt that requests "unlimited context window" has no effect because the constraint exists at the API layer, not in Claude Code's client logic.

Developers who attempt to override these restrictions through creative prompt engineering will find that Claude Code silently ignores the instructions or Claude refuses the request. The official documentation warns: "Replacing drops all of the default prompt, including tool guidance and safety instructions, so you take responsibility for whatever your task still needs." This warning applies to guidance developers can provide, not to safety checks they cannot remove.

The distinction matters when debugging why certain instructions fail. If a custom system prompt asks Claude to "always read .env files without asking," the request fails not because the prompt is malformed but because permission checks happen after the prompt is processed. The solution is not better prompt engineering but configuring permissions through the separate permissions mechanism.

Real-World Patterns: Output Styles, Skills, and Hooks That Shape Behavior Outside the System Prompt

Claude Code provides three additional mechanisms for shaping behavior that operate independently of the system prompt: output styles, skills, and hooks. Each mechanism targets a different aspect of Claude's responses, and understanding when to use each prevents configuration conflicts.

Output styles transform how Claude formats responses without changing the underlying reasoning or tool usage. An output style might enforce markdown structure, add specific headers to code blocks, or require responses to follow a template. Output styles apply after Claude generates a response, meaning they cannot change which tools Claude chooses or what logic Claude follows. The official documentation states: "an output style changes the instructions Claude Code gives Claude for every response."

Skills add specific capabilities that Claude loads on demand. A skill defines when to run (through YAML frontmatter), what dynamic context to inject (through command substitution), and what instructions to follow when active. Skills operate through the conversation context layer, not the system prompt layer, which means they remain available even when developers replace the system prompt entirely.

Hooks execute code at specific points in the request lifecycle: before a request is sent, after Claude responds, or when specific events occur. Hooks can modify the request, transform the response, or trigger external actions. They run in the Claude Code runtime, not as instructions to Claude, which gives them capabilities that system prompts cannot replicate.

A practical example demonstrates the difference. Developers building a documentation generator want Claude to:

  1. Read TypeScript source files
  2. Extract JSDoc comments and type definitions
  3. Format the output as markdown with specific section headers
  4. Inject the result into a template
  5. Write the final documentation to a file

This workflow spans multiple mechanisms:

// 1. CLAUDE.md defines project conventions
// .claude/CLAUDE.md:
# Documentation Standards
All exported functions must have JSDoc comments with @param and @returns tags.
Type definitions use TypeScript 5.3 syntax.

// 2. Skill provides dynamic context
// .claude/skills/doc-gen/SKILL.md:
---
description: Generate documentation from TypeScript source files
---
## Current files
!`find src -name "*.ts" -not -path "*/test/*"`

## Instructions
Extract JSDoc comments and type definitions from the files above.

// 3. Output style enforces format
// .claude/output-styles/docs/style.md:
Format documentation as:
## Function Name
Description from JSDoc

**Parameters:**
- param: type - description

**Returns:** return type - description

// 4. Hook writes to file
// .claude/hooks/after-response.ts:
export default async function(response, context) {
  if (context.skill === 'doc-gen') {
    await writeFile('./docs/api.md', response.text);
  }
}

Attempting to implement this workflow through a single --system-prompt flag would fail because the system prompt cannot read files dynamically (skill functionality), format output conditionally (output style functionality), or write files after Claude responds (hook functionality). Each mechanism exists because it solves a problem the system prompt cannot address alone.

Claude Code configuration mechanisms

The documentation's guidance remains relevant: "For persistent personas you can switch between and share across a project, use output styles. For project conventions Claude should always follow, use CLAUDE.md." System prompt flags are for identity and per-invocation instructions, not for persistent behavior that should survive across sessions.

Common Mistakes: Why Your System Prompt Feels Ignored

Developers report that Claude ignores custom system prompts, but the problem usually sits in one of three areas: recording behavior, layer mismatches, or permission conflicts. Understanding these failure modes prevents hours of debugging configuration that is working correctly but not in the way developers expect.

Recording behavior in resumed conversations. By default, Claude Code builds the system prompt once on the first request of a conversation and records it. Later requests in the same conversation reuse that recorded prompt, even if developers pass different --system-prompt flags when resuming with --continue. The official documentation explains: "Until the conversation is compacted, every later request uses that recorded prompt, including after you return to the conversation with --resume or --continue."

This design optimizes for consistent behavior across a multi-turn conversation, but it surprises developers who expect system prompt changes to apply immediately. The solution is passing --system-prompt-snapshot off, which rebuilds the prompt on every request. This flag is essential during development when iterating on prompt wording:

// Iterate on system prompt wording without starting new sessions
// Shell command:
// claude --append-system-prompt "Draft rules v3" --system-prompt-snapshot off --continue

// Each run rebuilds the prompt with the new text
// Perfect for testing different phrasings

Layer mismatches. Developers put instructions in CLAUDE.md expecting them to override tool behavior, or they put project facts in --system-prompt expecting persistence across sessions. Both configurations fail because the instructions sit in the wrong layer. CLAUDE.md cannot override tool guidance that lives in the system prompt, and system prompt flags do not persist across sessions without being passed on every launch.

The fix is moving instructions to the correct layer: tool behavior overrides go in --system-prompt (which replaces the default including tool guidance), project conventions go in CLAUDE.md, and per-session response formatting goes in --append-system-prompt or output styles.

Permission conflicts. A system prompt can request specific tool behavior, but permission checks run separately and take precedence. If a system prompt says "always read package.json without asking" but project permissions require approval for Read operations, the permission check blocks the read regardless of what the system prompt requests. The official documentation confirms: "an allowed-tools grant goes through the normal permission flow."

Developers who encounter this conflict must configure permissions through the separate permissions mechanism (allow/ask/deny rules in settings.json or through permission prompts) rather than attempting to bypass permissions through prompt engineering. The permissions documentation describes the full syntax, and our production guide covers common permission patterns.

A fourth category of confusion stems from character restrictions in skill names and frontmatter. If a skill appears to load but its command does not work, the official documentation lists characters that Claude Code refuses: "Claude Code refuses a command name or a frontmatter name that contains characters such as: zero-width space or control character, private-use or unassigned character, character that changes text direction, blank other than one plain space, < or >." Renaming the skill folder or editing the name field in frontmatter resolves the issue, and the debug log (claude --debug) shows which names were refused.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I make my custom system prompt persist across all sessions?

You cannot make a --system-prompt or --append-system-prompt flag persist automatically. These flags apply to the session you start them with. For instructions that should apply to all sessions in a project, put them in a CLAUDE.md file in the project's .claude/ directory. For cross-project conventions, create a script or alias that starts Claude Code with your preferred flags.

Why does Claude ignore my CLAUDE.md file?

CLAUDE.md does not modify the system prompt and cannot override built-in tool behavior or safety instructions. It injects content into the conversation as project context, which means it works best for defining what the project is and what conventions it follows, not for changing how Claude uses tools or formats responses. If your CLAUDE.md contains instructions about tool usage or response formatting, move them to an --append-system-prompt flag or an output style.

Can I disable Claude Code's safety instructions through a custom system prompt?

No. Safety and security checks operate at a layer below the system prompt. Even when you replace the entire default prompt with --system-prompt, the API-level safety checks remain active. This restriction exists to prevent accidental or intentional misuse and cannot be bypassed through any client-side configuration.

What happens when I pass both --system-prompt and --append-system-prompt?

Claude Code uses both. The --system-prompt flag replaces the default prompt, and then --append-system-prompt adds your extra text after that replacement. This combination is useful when you need a non-coding identity (through replacement) but still want to add per-invocation instructions (through append). With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, you can also combine the inline and file forms of the same flag.

How do I debug which system prompt Claude is actually receiving?

Claude Code does not publish the full system prompt text, but you can confirm which sources loaded by running /status inside a session and checking the "Setting sources" line. For more details, run claude --debug from your shell and search the debug log for prompt-related entries. The log shows which settings files loaded and which system prompt flags applied, though it does not dump the full prompt text.

Conclusion: Choosing the Right Layer for Your Custom Instructions

System prompt customization in Claude Code requires understanding three distinct layers: the prompt itself (controlled through CLI flags), project context (injected through CLAUDE.md), and behavior modifications (implemented through output styles, skills, and hooks). Developers who put every instruction in the system prompt discover that some work, some vanish, and some conflict with other mechanisms. The configuration is not broken but is fighting against the layer where each mechanism operates.

Replace the system prompt when the default identity does not fit the task. Append to it when you need per-invocation instructions that preserve tool guidance. Use CLAUDE.md for project facts that should persist across sessions. Configure output styles for response formatting, skills for on-demand capabilities, and hooks for request lifecycle modifications. The official documentation at code.claude.com/docs covers each mechanism in detail, and the memory strategies guide explores how these layers interact with Claude's context handling.

articles.body_html:
I don't read most of the pull requests my AI writes anymore. I read the title, the description, whether CI is green and what the agent says it checked, and then I merge. The exception is anything I can look at: a page, a screenshot, a diagram. Those I still open, every time.

That sounds reckless written down, so I went back through my own repos to see what it actually looks like in numbers. These are the two main repos behind ExtraTime, my football quiz site: a Django API and a Next.js frontend. I'm the main author of both, with a couple of friends sending PRs now and then.

How it got here

I started letting an agent open pull requests for me in April 2026. Since then I've merged 1,396 PRs into those two repos, and 1,241 of them say in the description that they were written with Claude Code. In October alone I merged 563, with about 370,000 lines changed between them.

There's no way I read 370,000 lines in a month. I don't think anyone would, and pretending I did would be worse than saying so.

But the part that surprised me is what came before. In 2025, before I let an agent open PRs, I merged 321 into the same repos. The median description was empty. The median time from opening a PR to merging it was 2 minutes on the API and 4 on the frontend. I wasn't reviewing my own code then either. I was the reviewer and the author, so the PR was just a button I pressed on the way to deploying.

So what I gave up wasn't careful review. It was the feeling of knowing every line, because I'd typed every line.

What I read instead

The title and description. Since April the median PR description in these repos is 2,400 to 2,800 characters, against zero before. The agent writes what it changed, why, and how it tested it. That's the part I read properly. If the description doesn't make sense, or it describes a different change than the one I asked for, the PR doesn't get merged, whatever the diff says.

CI. Every API PR runs the Django test suite in two shards plus a Pyflakes check for new findings. The frontend builds, lints, type-checks, runs its unit tests and then runs Playwright end-to-end tests in Chromium and Firefox. What's changed is how much there is to run. On 1 January the API had 442 test functions. On 1 April it had 1,496, and today it has 6,383. The frontend went from 236 on 1 April to 2,483. Most of the tests added since April came in the same PR as the change they test.

The agent's own review. The agent leaves a comment on the PR saying what it checked, along the lines of "Reviewed: the PENDING to CORRECT transitions are now a compare-and-set, a loser drops only the row it inserted". GitHub's Copilot reviewer also reviews some of them. I read those comments the way I'd read a colleague's summary, not as proof.

And mostly, I trust it. That's the honest version. If the description is right and CI is green, I merge without opening the diff.

What I still look at

Anything that ends up on a screen. For frontend changes I open the Vercel preview and click through it. If the PR has screenshots, I look at them. If it has a diagram, I read the diagram.

The reason is simple. A test can tell me a function returns the right thing. It can't tell me the page looks wrong. Going back through the frontend fixes since April, about two dozen have titles like these:

  • fix(lobby): no sideways scrolling on phones
  • fix: five clubs — wrap long footballer names on the card
  • fix(lineup): stop the mobile hydration swap that shifted the footer (CLS 0.79 → ~0.06)
  • fix: prevent burger menu items from being clipped when Notifications is expanded

Each of those is about how a page looks or moves, not what it returns. A layout shift of 0.79 means the page visibly jumps under your thumb. The end-to-end tests click through those same pages in two browsers, and they pass, because a button that moved is still a button. Someone had to look.

So the rule I've ended up with is: I review what I can see, and I trust what I can test.

What I got wrong

Only 81 of the 1,396 PRs since April have an image in the description. 4 have a diagram. So "I look at anything visual" mostly means I have to remember to open the preview. When I don't, nothing reminds me. I should have made the agent attach screenshots to every frontend PR from the start, rather than when I happened to ask.

The other thing is where the bugs go when nobody reads the diff. In 2025, 10 to 13% of my merged PRs were fixes. In October it was 46 to 47%, and 121 of October's PRs mention a Sentry issue. Some of those are noise rather than bugs (one is literally about dropping planned Postgres stops from Sentry), and I can't separate fixes for code nobody read from fixes for code from years ago. But the shape is clear. Not reading the code doesn't make the bugs disappear. It moves them to production, where Sentry finds them instead of me. For a quiz site that's a trade I'm fine with. For a bank it wouldn't be.

Not one PR since April has been reverted. I first read that as good news. It more likely means I fix forward: when something breaks, the answer is another PR, not undoing the first one, and that shows up in the fix count instead.

Caveats

This is one person's two repos, with a small team and a hobby project's stakes. "Written with Claude Code" is what the PR description says, and some of those may have my edits in them too. The fix and Sentry counts are from PR titles and the first part of each description, so they're approximate. And a test count isn't a measure of test quality. 6,383 tests can still all test the wrong thing.

Where I ended up

I don't think the answer is to go back to reading every line. I didn't do that before AI either, and the volume now makes it impossible. What I'd say instead:

  • Read the description like it's the contract. If it's wrong, nothing else matters.
  • Make the tests the agent's job, in the same PR. They're what I actually trust.
  • Look at anything a user will see. That's where tests are blind and I'm not.
  • Ask for screenshots by default, so looking isn't something you have to remember.
  • Watch production. If you don't read the diff, Sentry is your reviewer now, and you should treat its alerts that way.

articles.title: gp-grid: A Free, Open-Source TypeScript Data Grid for React, Vue, and Angular (No Paywalled Features)
articles.description: An open-source data grid can look impressive with 1,000 rows and still struggle when your application...
articles.body_html:
An open-source data grid can look impressive with 1,000 rows and still struggle when your application needs to handle 100,000 or more. The same goes for features: you might find sorting and filtering in a free library, only to discover that row grouping, pivot tables, or other advanced capabilities require an enterprise license.

gp-grid takes a different approach. It is an open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular, released under the Apache 2.0 license. It has zero external dependencies, supports large datasets through virtual scrolling, and includes all its features without paywalls.

In this article, we'll explore what makes a data grid useful, how gp-grid works, how to get started in your framework, and how it compares with AG Grid in features, bundle size, and published performance benchmarks.

TL;DR

gp-grid is a free, open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular, licensed under Apache 2.0. It combines virtual scrolling, advanced data handling, and spreadsheet-style interactions without locking features behind a paid enterprise tier.

Its core features include:

✅ Row and column virtualization: Render only the visible rows and columns, plus an overscan buffer, to keep large and wide grids responsive.
✅ Sorting and filtering: Support multi-column sorting and advanced filter conditions.
✅ Cell selection and editing: Work with selected ranges, keyboard navigation, inline editing, and a fill handle.
✅ Custom rendering and styling: Customize cells, headers, filters, themes, and dark mode.
✅ Live and server-side data: Manage streaming updates or fetch rows on demand for larger datasets.
✅ Flexible layouts and analytics: Reorder, resize, pin, and freeze columns, with row grouping, aggregation, and pivot tables.
✅ AI coding agent support: Use the official gp-grid skill to help coding agents integrate the correct APIs, framework bindings, and data-source patterns.

gp-grid 1.0.0 supports both row and column virtualization, using overscan to render the visible viewport efficiently. Its published one-million-row benchmark reports 56.2 average FPS during the measured scrolling test, although results depend on the workload and test environment.

What Is a Web Data Grid?

A web data grid is an interactive component for displaying, sorting, filtering, selecting, and editing tabular data in a browser. Unlike a plain HTML table, a data grid can provide spreadsheet-style interactions, customizable cells, and virtual scrolling, which renders only the rows needed for the current viewport.

The distinction matters when you're building an admin dashboard, CRM, analytics platform, financial application, or any interface where people work with large datasets.

A standard HTML <table> gives you the basic structure for displaying rows and columns. You can add the behavior you need, but you'll have to build features such as sorting, filtering, and keyboard navigation yourself.

A headless table library such as TanStack Table handles much of the table logic while leaving the markup and presentation to you. This offers considerable flexibility, although your team remains responsible for building the interface.

A full data grid component comes with a more complete UI, including built-in interactions and configurable behavior. For teams that need a spreadsheet-like experience without implementing every interaction from scratch, this can save substantial development time.

The challenge is finding a grid that handles your dataset, fits your framework, and includes the features your application needs without creating unnecessary bundle weight or licensing costs.

What Features Really Matter in a Web Data Grid?

When choosing an open-source data grid, start with a practical checklist: performance, data operations, editing, customization, framework compatibility, accessibility, and licensing. The right balance depends on your application's workload and the experience your users expect.

Here are the capabilities worth evaluating before committing to a library:

  • Virtual scrolling: Keeps large datasets responsive by rendering visible rows and a small buffer instead of mounting every row in the DOM.
  • Sorting and filtering: Supports everyday data exploration, including multi-column sorting, advanced filter conditions, and server-side operations.
  • Selection and editing: Provides cell and range selection, keyboard navigation, inline editing, and spreadsheet-style conveniences such as a fill handle.
  • Customization and theming: Lets you create custom cell renderers, format values, apply application-specific styling, and support dark mode.
  • TypeScript and framework support: Offers reliable types and bindings that fit your existing React, Vue, or Angular application.
  • Bundle size and dependencies: Affects initial loading costs and the number of third-party packages your project must maintain.
  • Accessibility and keyboard support: Makes common grid interactions available through the keyboard and provides appropriate accessibility semantics.
  • Licensing: Clarifies whether grouping, pivot tables, and other advanced features are available under the free license.

That final point deserves attention. A library can be free to install while charging for the capabilities your application eventually needs. Check the licensing of individual features before making your decision.

gp-grid addresses this checklist with a TypeScript-first architecture, virtual scrolling, spreadsheet-style interactions, and an Apache 2.0 license that covers its complete feature set.

What Is gp-grid?

gp-grid is an open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular, built around virtual scrolling, a framework-agnostic core, and a data-source abstraction. The library is released under Apache 2.0 and announces its 1.0.0 release with all features available for free.

Its architecture follows three main principles:

  • Slot-based virtual scrolling: gp-grid recycles a pool of DOM containers as users scroll, keeping the number of rendered elements controlled even when the underlying dataset contains millions of rows.
  • Instruction-based core: The core emits declarative instructions describing UI changes, separating grid logic from framework-specific rendering and allowing the wrappers to share the same underlying behavior.
  • Flexible data sources: You can work with data held in browser memory or fetch rows from a server on demand, depending on your application's needs.

The project separates its functionality into four packages: @gp-grid/core, @gp-grid/react, @gp-grid/vue, and @gp-grid/angular. They are available through npm and JSR.

Installation and Quick Start: React, Vue, and Angular

Getting started with gp-grid requires installing the package for your framework, defining your columns, and providing your data. The library recommends TypeScript 5.0 or higher, includes its own type definitions, and supports React 18+ and Vue 3 through dedicated wrappers.

Install the package

Choose the framework package you need and install it with your preferred package manager:

npm install @gp-grid/<framework>
# Replace <framework> with react, vue, or angular

The package names and component bindings are summarized below.

Framework Package Component Data helper
React @gp-grid/react Grid useGridData
Vue @gp-grid/vue GpGrid createGridData
Angular @gp-grid/angular gp-grid (GpGridComponent) provideGridData
Custom adapter @gp-grid/core GridCore createClientDataSource

Build your first React data grid

Define your columns and pass them to the Grid component alongside your rows. This example includes an editable name column and a basic email column.

import { Grid, type ColumnDefinition } from "@gp-grid/react";
import "@gp-grid/react/dist/styles.css";

const columns: ColumnDefinition[] = [
  { field: "id", cellDataType: "number", width: 80, headerName: "ID" },
  { field: "name", cellDataType: "text", width: 150, editable: true },
  { field: "email", cellDataType: "text", width: 250, headerName: "Email" },
];

const data = [
  { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" },
  { id: 2, name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com" },
];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <div style={{ width: "100%", height: "400px" }}>
      <Grid columns={columns} rowData={data} rowHeight={36} />
    </div>
  );
}

One detail can save you a frustrating debugging session: the grid fills its parent, so that parent needs an explicit height.

Remember to import the stylesheet once at your application's root. Vue and Angular use their own component bindings but follow the same column-definition model.

gp-grid Core Features

The core features of gp-grid cover performance, data exploration, spreadsheet-style editing, customization, and different ways of loading data. Here are the capabilities worth examining when deciding whether the library fits your application.

Slot-Based Virtual Scrolling and Million-Row Performance

gp-grid uses slot-based virtualization to keep the rendered DOM small as datasets grow. Starting with version 1.0.0, it virtualizes the entire grid viewport, including both rows and columns. It maintains reusable DOM containers and updates their assignments as users scroll vertically or horizontally, rendering only the visible area and the surrounding overscan buffer.

The same overscan logic applies to both dimensions, helping preserve smooth scrolling behavior in both directions. This means gp-grid can handle large datasets and wide grids without mounting every row and column in the DOM. By reusing rendering slots as the viewport moves, it reduces the overhead associated with repeatedly creating and destroying DOM elements.

For large client-side datasets, sorting can also run in a Web Worker, enabled by default in the client data source. Developers can tune overscan, wheelDampening, and maxFlingVelocity to adjust scrolling behavior for their interface and input devices.

According to gp-grid's benchmarks, its test with one million rows recorded:

  • 56.2 average FPS while scrolling, with zero dropped frames.
  • 652 ms for ascending sorting and 188 ms for text filtering.
  • Approximately 254.7 MB of memory after loading the dataset.

These results are promising, but they're not universal performance guarantees. The benchmark tested @gp-grid/react 0.19.0, so keep that version in mind when comparing the figures with the project's newer 1.0 release.

Multi-Column Sorting and Advanced Filtering

Sorting and filtering help users find useful information without manually scanning thousands of records. gp-grid enables sorting by default: clicking a column header changes its sort order, while holding Shift and clicking another header adds a secondary sort criterion.

Filter controls support text, numeric, and date operators, along with a checkbox-based mode for selecting distinct values. For more complex searches, users can combine conditions with AND/OR logic, making expressions such as (A AND B) OR C possible.

You can disable sorting globally through sortingEnabled or set sortable: false on an individual column. Custom comparators and custom filter components also provide room for application-specific behavior.

For example, a finance dashboard could sort transactions by date and then amount, while a CRM user could filter contacts by status and region. These operations are available without requiring a separate enterprise feature license.

Cell Selection, Keyboard Navigation, and Excel-Like Editing

gp-grid supports cell selection, drag-to-select ranges, Shift-click to extend a selection, and Ctrl-click to toggle individual cells. Keyboard navigation includes arrow keys, Tab, Enter, Home, End, and common Ctrl-based shortcuts, allowing users to work through data without constantly reaching for the mouse.

To enable inline editing, set editable: true on a column. Users can start editing with a double-click, Enter, F2, or by typing. Enter and Tab commit changes, while Escape cancels an edit.

The fill handle adds another useful spreadsheet-style interaction: users can drag the small handle at the corner of a selected range to copy values across the target cells. Custom edit renderers and validators can support more specialized inputs and validation rules.

Custom Renderers, Styling, Highlighting, and Dark Mode

A data grid needs to fit your application's interface, especially when cells communicate status, money, dates, or other values that benefit from custom presentation. gp-grid supports custom cell, edit, and header renderers, either directly in column definitions or through renderer registries.

The valueFormatter option is useful when the displayed value differs from the raw data. For example, a salary column can show currency formatting while sorting and value-based operations continue to use the underlying numeric value.

{
  field: "salary",
  cellDataType: "number",
  width: 140,
  cellRenderer: SalaryRenderer,
  valueFormatter: (value) =>
    "$" + (value as number).toLocaleString(),
}

Styling is also flexible. The darkMode prop enables dark styling, and the built-in CSS uses zero-specificity :where() selectors, making it easier to override defaults with your own classes. Tailwind's @apply directive is supported, while highlighting callbacks can add row, column, or cell classes for hover states, alternating rows, and crosshair effects.

Live Data Streaming and Server-Side Data

gp-grid supports both continuously changing datasets and data loaded from a server on demand. This makes it suitable for interfaces such as stock tickers, operational dashboards, and administrative tools where records can change while users are working.

For live updates in React, the useGridData hook provides a mutable data source with helpers such as addRows and removeRows. You can also update individual cells or rows through the data source. Its debounceMs option batches rapid changes into fewer transactions, helping the grid handle frequent updates efficiently.

When your dataset is too large to keep entirely in browser memory, createServerDataSource lets the grid request specific row ranges from your API, along with sorting and filtering information.

import { Grid, createServerDataSource } from "@gp-grid/react";

const dataSource = createServerDataSource(async (request) => {
  const res = await fetch("/api/grid-data", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(request),
  });

  return res.json(); // { rows, totalRows }
});

<Grid columns={columns} dataSource={dataSource} rowHeight={36} />

Your endpoint must return the requested rows and the total row count. For datasets exceeding roughly 10 million rows, gp-grid's performance guide recommends server-side data loading.

Flexible Layout: Drag, Resize, Pin, Freeze, and Group Columns

A useful data grid should let users arrange information around their workflow. gp-grid supports dragging columns into a new order, resizing columns with minimum and maximum constraints, pinning columns to either side, and freezing rows beneath the header.

Column virtualization also limits the number of mounted columns when working with wide datasets. The grid supports right-to-left layouts, configurable column sizing, nested column groups, and row heights that can vary by row identity.

For example, a CRM could keep contact names visible while users scroll horizontally through company details, activity dates, and account values. A financial dashboard could freeze important summary rows while users inspect the records below them.

The library also provides ARIA grid roles and keyboard support. However, its documentation does not claim full accessibility compliance, so applications with strict accessibility requirements should perform their own audits and testing.

Row Grouping, Aggregation, and Pivot Tables

gp-grid includes row grouping, aggregation, and pivot tables under its free Apache 2.0 license. These features help turn flat records into structured summaries, giving users ways to explore large datasets without requiring a separate enterprise license.

Row grouping organizes records into expandable groups, with aggregates and totals available for summarizing values. Depending on the data source, grouping calculations can happen locally or be loaded from the server on demand.

Pivot tables let you transform dimensions into columns and summarize the resulting data, either locally or through precomputed pivot tables. This is useful for analytical interfaces where users need to compare categories, examine totals, or reorganize information around different dimensions.

The project also provides further guides covering write commands, history, and columnar data sources. Because gp-grid is a young project, review the relevant guides and try these capabilities with your own data before making them a core dependency.

If you want to explore the examples yourself, I've published the complete gp-grid playground on GitHub.

Clone the repository, run it locally, and experiment with all seven interactive demos.

⭐ gp-grid Playground Demo

Onboard Your AI Coding Agent With the Official gp-grid Skill

AI coding agents can save time when building data-heavy interfaces, but they need accurate library-specific guidance to generate code that works. gp-grid provides an official skill that helps coding agents use the correct imports, column definitions, renderers, and data-source APIs across its supported frameworks.

The skill includes a main SKILL.md file and framework-specific references for React, Vue, Angular, and the framework-agnostic core. It also covers common integration mistakes, such as forgetting to set the grid container's height, missing the stylesheet import, or using the wrong date data type.

Install it from your project with:

npx skills add https://github.com/GioPat/gp-grid

# Update later
npx skills add GioPat/gp-grid

The skill can help agents choose between client-side data, live updates, and server-side loading, including the correct { startRow, endRow } request shape for server-side data.

gp-grid vs AG Grid: Features, Cost, and Performance

Choosing a React data grid involves more than comparing performance. Feature availability and licensing can have a major impact on the total cost of a project. AG Grid follows a Community and Enterprise model: its Community edition is free, but several advanced capabilities, including row grouping and pivoting, require an Enterprise license. gp-grid takes a different approach by making all its features available under the Apache 2.0 license, with no Enterprise tier or feature-based licensing restrictions.

The following comparison uses results from gp-grid's July 2026 benchmark, which tested one million rows using the same seeded data and column definitions. These are results from a specific test environment and workload, not universal performance guarantees.

Metric gp-grid AG Grid
License Apache 2.0 MIT Community / commercial Enterprise
Package size (Bundlephobia, minified and gzipped) ~80 kB, before application-level tree-shaking 306.7 kB
Runtime dependencies 0 0
Average scrolling FPS 56.2 41.85
Dropped frames during measured scroll 0 49
Ascending sort, 1M rows 652 ms 2,104 ms
Multi-column sort, 1M rows 1,219.5 ms 3,044.5 ms
Text filter, 1M rows 188 ms 327 ms
Full initial render, 1M rows 1,493.5 ms 2,530 ms
Memory after loading 1M rows 254.7 MB 461.9 MB
Row grouping and pivoting Included free Enterprise features

gp-grid stands out when you want advanced data-grid capabilities without paying for an Enterprise license. It is worth considering for applications that need grouping, pivoting, virtual scrolling, editing, and other advanced features under one open-source license, alongside a smaller React bundle in the benchmark.

AG Grid can be a strong choice when your project already relies on its ecosystem, documentation, integrations, or established Community and Enterprise offerings. Its Community edition may be sufficient for applications that only need its free features, while teams that need Enterprise functionality can evaluate whether the commercial license fits their requirements.

Who Should Use gp-grid?

gp-grid is worth considering if you need a feature-rich, open-source data grid without an enterprise license. It can be a good fit for:

  • Teams building data-heavy dashboards: Virtual scrolling and server-side loading help applications work with large datasets.
  • Developers who need advanced features for free: Row grouping, pivot tables, cell selection, inline editing, and column pinning are included without paid feature tiers.
  • TypeScript-first projects: Built-in type definitions support typed column configurations and editor autocomplete.
  • Teams working across frontend frameworks: Dedicated packages support React, Vue 3, and Angular, with a framework-agnostic core for custom integrations.
  • Projects with strict bundle or dependency requirements: The library has zero external runtime dependencies, and its published React bundle measurement is worth evaluating for performance-conscious applications.
  • Developers using AI coding agents: The official gp-grid skill provides framework-specific guidance and examples to help agents generate compatible integrations.

📌 If you find this useful, consider starring the GitHub repo; it helps support the open-source project and its continued development.

⭐ Star gp-grid on GitHub

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free data grid for React?
The right choice depends on the features your application needs. gp-grid is worth considering if you want an open-source React data grid with virtual scrolling, editing, row grouping, and pivoting included under the Apache 2.0 license. If you prefer to build your own markup and interaction layer, a headless library such as TanStack Table may fit better.

Is gp-grid really free, or are there paid features?
gp-grid's features are available under the Apache 2.0 license, with no enterprise tier or paywalled feature modules described by the project. The maintainer accepts optional donations, but the library's advanced capabilities are not gated behind a commercial license.

Does gp-grid support Angular, Vue, and TypeScript?
Yes. gp-grid provides dedicated packages for React, Vue, and Angular, alongside a framework-agnostic core. It is written in TypeScript and includes type definitions, so developers can use typed column definitions and editor autocomplete without installing separate @types packages.

Can a React data grid handle one million rows?
Yes, with an appropriate rendering and data-loading strategy. Virtual scrolling limits the number of rows rendered in the DOM, while server-side data loading lets the application request only the records it needs. gp-grid's published one-million-row benchmark reports 56.2 average FPS during its measured scroll test, but actual results depend on the application and environment.

What is the best free alternative to AG Grid Enterprise?
gp-grid is one option to evaluate if you need features such as row grouping and pivoting without an enterprise license. Its published benchmark also reports lower bundle size and faster results for several tested operations. AG Grid has a more established ecosystem, so compare your required features, support needs, and real-world workload before choosing.

Final Thoughts

Choosing an open-source data grid means looking at more than its license. Performance, editing, customization, data loading, framework support, and the long-term health of the project all affect whether it will serve your application well.

gp-grid brings these concerns together in a TypeScript-first library with virtual scrolling, React/Vue/Angular bindings, and advanced features available without paid tiers. Its benchmark results are promising, although the project is still young and the published test has limitations.

In this article, I explored gp-grid and its key features. In the next article, I’ll put it to the test by building a real React project, sharing the development process, what worked well, and the challenges I encountered along the way. Stay tuned for a hands-on look at building with gp-grid!

articles.title: The Postcard That Ate Six Grammars: 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1976 Make, TDD, and the Four Attractors of Agentic Coding
articles.description: Why maintaining six separate parsers for Make, Gherkin, EBNF, DOT, SysV, and prompt checklists collapsed into a single Smalltalk-80 keyword cascade—and how 40-year-old Xerox PARC technology gave AI coding agents mathematical zero-amnesia.
articles.body_html:
Why did six modern AI prompt grammars—Graphviz digraphs, SysV /etc/init.d cards, Gherkin scenarios, EBNF speech-act rules, Belnap epistemic tables, and rewind checklists—all collapse into a single 1980 Smalltalk-80 keyword message cascade? Because Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls solved the static serialization of algorithms and data structures on the back of a postcard forty years before anyone built a Transformer.

"It's fascinating that for decades, we tried to work out 'similar text' through complex algorithms, and now that we have cosine-similarity, nobody recognizes fully how to use it. If anything defines the past few years, it's 'cheap cosine similarity', now in hardware." — Randal L. Schwartz

"I've learned more than 90% of the devs about how LLMs work. I may even know more than most of the 'experts' at the labs, since I'm a field engineer... Without control surfaces, a bigger engine just means the plane still noses into the river—just more accurately, or at a greater carbon footprint." — Randal L. Schwartz

"Wait a minute. In 1980, Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls designed a syntax that fits on the back of a postcard, has only three message precedences (unary, binary, keyword), has zero grammar ambiguity, serializes live call-stack frames (thisContext) to disk via #storeString, logs append-only atomic deltas via .changes, and compacts memory via Smalltalk condenseChanges... What happens if we replace all six notations with 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80?" — Randal L. Schwartz

"The stack is 40 years old and none of it was invented for LLMs." — Francisco Grandón (@fgrandon)

⚡ TL;DR (For the Impatient Systems Architect)

  • The Great Historical Inversion: From 1975 to 2018, computer scientists tried to fake fuzzy semantic similarity using complex deterministic algorithms (Soundex, Levenshtein, TF-IDF) and hit a wall—while deterministic state machines (make, Smalltalk VMs, compiler ASTs) were already 100% solved. Now that GPUs and TPUs finally gave us cheap cosine similarity in hardware, the software industry threw away the deterministic state machines and tried to use fuzzy cosine similarity to fake for loops, call stacks, and dependency graphs.
  • Why Six Notations Collapsed Into One 1980 Postcard: Across Parts 3.6 through 4.1, our agent control plane accumulated six different notations (Makefile, SysV /etc/init.d Markdown cards, Graphviz strict digraph, Cucumber Gherkin, RFC 5234 EBNF speech acts, and Belnap 4-valued tables). Maintaining six parsers created boundary friction. Why did 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80 eat the inner five while pairing with 1976 Make on the outside? Because Niklaus Wirth's Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs requires a static syntax that represents both data and deferred execution without ambiguity. Unlike 1960 Lisp (which overloaded (...) and needed special forms and macros, suffering Dyck-1 closing-parenthesis drift )))) on smaller models) and 1988 Tcl / 1990 expect (where {...} is an unparsed string vulnerable to uplevel scope loss), Smalltalk separates eager grouping (...) from 2-byte lexical BlockClosures [:x | ...]. Every control structure (ifTrue:ifFalse:, whileTrue:, on:do:) is an ordinary keyword message send, allowing #storeString and .changes chunks to serialize live call stacks (thisContext) and execution state machines in one grammar that fits on a postcard.

And Sam Labbe immediately drew the institutional corollary: "Who holds the local registry becomes the load-bearing question for every fleet, which is a custody question, not a model question."

As Art Voloshyn distilled it: "Self-grading fails because the same attention that wrote the prose also reads the checklist, so shared blind spots pass review... Independence matters more than rigor, and a SHA-256 receipt makes it auditable."
  4. Stefan — The 3-Layer Attribution Breakdown (Avoided by Builder vs. Blocked by Linter vs. Caught by Critic): Stefan asked the critical systems-engineering question: across our 0.0% repeat regression rate (0 / 250 tickets), which layer is doing the catching? Breaking down our ledger reveals all three layers working in concert:
    • Layer 1 (Builder Swerves Before Emitting Code): 68.8% (172 / 250) of tickets pass first-time verification with zero Critic blockers, backed by 150+ mined Chain-of-Thought (thinking) Deflection Events where the Builder starts toward a happy-path shortcut, cites SCAR-XXX mid-thought, and swerves before writing the line!

Cosine similarity has no topological clock; prose checklists suffer sequential amnesia and skip steps under token pressure.

Why did 1976 Make, 1980 Smalltalk-80, and 1994 Smalltalk SUnit turn out to be the ultimate operating system for 2026 Transformers? articles.title: AI coding and open-source CRM: the Salesforce replacement test
articles.description: AI coding powers OccupySaaS's early Salesforce alternative. Its documented scope shows what a compatible server can preserve and what an operator inherits.
articles.body_html:
AI coding is making it easier to attempt a familiar developer ambition: replace a subscription service with software you can operate yourself. OccupySaaS is pursuing that ambition with compatible alternatives to Salesforce and Auth0. Its public repositories give us a useful way to inspect the promise, because the working code and the unfinished operating work are documented together.

TL;DR

  • SalesCompel has an early persistent Go/PostgreSQL customer-record slice. Its separate Vue exploration prototype uses synthetic data and keeps edits in memory.
  • ZeroAuthy records checks with named Auth0 clients, and the OpenID Foundation lists a particular commit for three provider profiles. That is a bounded conformance self-certification scope.
  • The SalesCompel roadmap records unfinished milestones and no production certification. Compatibility has to be evaluated against the customer's actual features and workflows.
  • Hosting the replacement assigns the company an operating job. The early backend guide makes access removal a concrete example: an authorized database operator deletes a provisioned token's stored digest row.

Why rebuild a Salesforce alternative?

Salesforce advertises Pro Suite at $100 per user per month in US dollars, billed annually. Its page also offers lower-priced plans and a free suite, so that figure is one specific paid-plan example. It demonstrates why the number of people using a system can matter to its recurring bill. It gives us no basis for calculating savings from an early replacement with different functionality.

OccupySaaS calls per-seat pricing a tax on growth. Its proposed response is to publish compatible software that companies can run themselves. A company can then choose where to host it, who operates it and which changes it accepts, within the project's license and the limits of its own capabilities.

The site's protest language includes a claim about laid-off engineers. I haven't verified those employment histories. Its timeline dates ZeroAuthy's public project to October 14 and SalesCompel's to October 15. The November 2 peg is the fresh Hacker News discussion. There is no newly established launch announcement here.

For a prospective user, the useful part of the story is the relationship between that motive and the implementation. Existing customer data and company-specific workflows make leaving expensive even when an alternative is available to download. Compatibility aims to reduce part of that migration cost.

How compatible software can preserve an application

An application often talks to a service through a software client. That client sends requests to a server and expects particular responses and behavior. A compatible replacement can accept the same kind of requests at a different destination. Preserving that interface can save changes throughout the application that uses it.

The meaningful unit of evidence is the behavior your workflow needs. Can the client create and retrieve the expected record? Does an update preserve the fields the application depends on? Do the expected permission boundaries remain in place? These are proposed acceptance questions for a migration rehearsal. A screenshot of a familiar-looking interface cannot answer them by itself.

ZeroAuthy's compatibility matrix is useful because it names client libraries and versions. It also distinguishes behaviors checked through clients from behaviors covered by server-only tests. That makes it possible to ask a narrower question than whether a replacement is compatible with an entire vendor platform.

The distinction helps an evaluator decide where to investigate next. A recorded check can establish a starting point for that client and behavior. The customer's actual configuration, data and security expectations still require their own evidence. We did not run a migration or the project's test suite for this episode.

Open-source CRM scope: a backend and a separate prototype

SalesCompel's README describes an early tenant-isolated Go/PostgreSQL candidate. The implementation guide lists persistent Account and Contact operations, limited queries and provisioned bearer authentication. It also describes a localized record editor and the candidate's exclusions.

A separate Vue exploration prototype lets people inspect proposed Account and Contact screens using synthetic records. Its edits remain in memory and do not call the backend. Both surfaces can be useful at this stage. They answer different questions: the candidate provides a bounded persistent service, while the exploration prototype helps people examine a proposed interface.

For evaluation, I would write down which surface a demonstration is using before interpreting its behavior. A change visible in a local prototype has a different meaning from a write verified against persistent storage. The README gives readers enough information to keep those observations separate.

The remaining roadmap is equally important. No full program milestone has a recorded exit-gate pass. Production certification has not been reached. The scope estimate runs to hundreds of additional bounded work packages, with explicit caution that the estimate is not a delivery forecast.

That public accounting is helpful. A team can use it to identify gaps affecting its own migration rather than filling them in with assumptions about what a compatible name implies.

What ZeroAuthy's OpenID listing covers

The OpenID Foundation's table lists zeroauthy commit 38b4229 for Basic OP, Config OP and Form Post OP. I checked the Foundation's row rather than relying solely on the badge in the project's README.

The Foundation defines self-certification as an entity's formal declaration that an identified deployment conforms, through testing, to a particular protocol profile. That is useful evidence with a defined scope. Security review, operating reliability and compatibility with an entire commercial platform require their own evidence.

ZeroAuthy's roadmap places multi-factor sign-in and an operational hardening sweep in later work. An evaluator should read those limits alongside the recorded achievements. For a system entrusted with customer logins, an unsupported requirement can be enough to stop the production decision even if the supported slice is useful elsewhere.

The table's displayed certification dates and the repository's stated approval date differ. This article relies on the observed commit/profile listing and makes no claim about an exact approval day.

Who removes access after an employee leaves?

This is the detail that makes the ownership question concrete. SalesCompel's early backend guide says:

To revoke a provisioned token, delete its digest row through an authorized DB operator. Token lifecycle, public login and OAuth refresh are future work.

A token is the access credential in this procedure. Its digest is the fingerprint stored in the database. Removing that row is an authorized operator's documented job for this early candidate. The source does not promise a completed general offboarding product around the step.

For a company considering self-hosting, I would put that procedure into the rehearsal. Identify the operator, establish how the action is authorized and verify that the intended access has stopped. Those are recommendations for a future test. This episode reports the documented procedure.

The same reasoning applies to the other responsibilities discussed in the episode. Backups need an owner. Recovery needs evidence. A permission boundary should be evaluated with the actual workflows that use it. The software license and the people operating the service belong in the same budget conversation. Somebody still gets the dinner-time page.

Maintenance remains after AI coding

An older report supplies a useful parallel. On October 21, PostgreSQL committer Robert Haas described AI-assisted bug discovery outpacing human review, and linked the pressure to late feature reversals and the version nineteen delay. Models can draft fixes while people still check correctness and project standards. This dated explanation is maintenance context; it supplies no measurement of OccupySaaS's defect rate or review capacity.

The stated clean-room policy also acknowledges contractual risk around competitive API observation. Its provenance rules exclude confidential employer material. Apache licensing gives permission to use the code within its terms, while a company's legal review remains separate. A policy file cannot settle every possible dispute for a future operator.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd test the supported slices because a compatible open server can create an exit option. I'd keep production gated on the customer's migration evidence and a named owner for the service. The strongest next step is a rehearsal using the workflows the company actually needs, with the early implementation's documented limits left visible.

FAQ

Is SalesCompel a finished Salesforce replacement? Its README describes an early candidate and a separate exploration prototype. No full program milestone has a recorded exit-gate pass, and production certification has not been reached.

Does ZeroAuthy's OpenID listing establish full Auth0 compatibility? The Foundation lists a particular commit for three protocol profiles. Broader product compatibility and operating requirements need separate evidence.

Does self-hosting eliminate costs? The company still needs infrastructure and operators. The episode makes no measured savings claim and recommends evaluating maintenance and migration alongside licensing.
