articles.title: Your LoRa Board Can Track Airliners at 150 Nautical Miles
articles.description: The datasheet stops at 960 MHz. The airplanes are at 1090. Somebody did the math...
articles.body_html:
The datasheet stops at 960 MHz. The airplanes are at 1090. Somebody did the math anyway.

Somewhere over your house right now, a few dozen aircraft are shouting their names into the dark. Altitude, heading, a 24-bit hex identity, all of it on 1090 MHz, all of it plaintext, roughly twice a second, to anyone holding the right piece of copper. For about a decade the right piece of copper was an RTL-SDR dongle hanging off a Raspberry Pi. That arrangement still works. It's also no longer the cheapest way in.

On November 1, Hackaday covered a build by a developer who goes by thefatmoop: an ADS-B receiver made from a Meshnology W12 board, which pairs an ESP32-S3 with Semtech's new LR2021 LoRa transceiver. No SDR. No Linux. No Pi. The board demodulates the aircraft signal itself, checks the CRC, and serves live tracks on a web page from a chip the size of a postage stamp. The builder reports aircraft at around 150 nautical miles with an indoor antenna that was cut for the wrong band. Parts come in under $50.

That last detail is the interesting one. The radio was never sold to do this.

The Box Says 960 MHz

Pull up the LR2021 spec and you get two published frequency ranges: 150 to 960 MHz for the sub-GHz path, and 1600 to 2500 MHz for the 2.4 GHz and S-band side. ADS-B lives at 1090 MHz, which falls neatly in the gap between them, a dead zone on the marketing sheet.

The build tunes the sub-GHz path to 1090 anyway, and it hears airplanes.

There's a whole philosophy of hardware hiding in that sentence. A frequency range on a datasheet is a promise about performance across temperature, voltage and production lots. A warranty, basically. The synthesizer inside a modern transceiver usually has more headroom than the vendor wants to characterize, guarantee and support, so the published number lands where the lawyers and the test engineers are comfortable. Past that number you are on your own, which in practice means the thing usually works a little worse and nobody will help you when it doesn't.

Every interesting capability in computing started as a misuse. Wi-Fi chips became spectrum analyzers. TV tuner dongles became the RTL-SDR. Now a LoRa transceiver built for battery-powered sensor meshes is pulling Mode S out of the sky. The pins don't care what the box says. They care about tolerances.

The second reason this works is the modulation list. The LR2021 supports FSK, LoRa, LR-FHSS, FLRC, O-QPSK and OOK. That last one, on-off keying, is the whole trick, because ADS-B is pulses of carrier switched on and off. Strip away the aviation acronyms and an aircraft transponder is a very fast, very loud flashlight.

What a Plane Actually Says

ADS-B on 1090 MHz is called Extended Squitter. Each message opens with an 8 microsecond preamble: four short pulses at fixed offsets (0, 1.0, 3.5 and 4.5 microseconds) that work as a fingerprint for "a Mode S frame starts here." After the preamble comes the data block, 112 bits at one megabit per second.

The encoding is pulse position modulation. Each bit gets a 1 microsecond slot split into two halves. A pulse in the first half is a 1, a pulse in the second half is a 0. If that sounds like Manchester encoding riding on OOK, you've understood it, and that's exactly how the build's write-up describes it.

Inside those 112 bits:

DF   (5 bits)   downlink format, 17 for ADS-B from a transponder
CA   (3 bits)   capability
AA   (24 bits)  ICAO address, the aircraft's permanent hex identity
ME   (56 bits)  the payload: position, velocity, callsign, depending on type
PI   (24 bits)  CRC-24 parity

The CRC is your entire quality gate. At 1090 MHz you're listening to a crowded band full of overlapping replies, reflections and garbage, so the receiver lives or dies on rejecting frames that don't check out. The ESP32-S3 handles that in firmware: frames that fail the CRC go in the bin, frames that pass get decoded into tracks.

Note what's missing from that bit layout. There's no signature, no key and no nonce. The 2013 academic paper "On the Security of the Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast Protocol" said it plainly: the data link layer has no authentication. Anyone can listen, and nobody can tell you're listening. Keep that in mind, because it comes back at the end.

Flashing It

The project ships as a GPL-3.0 repository, esp32s3-lr2021-adsb-receiver, with a factory image in its releases. The flow is short enough to fit on a napkin:

1. flash the factory image (follow the repo's install guide)
2. join the W12-ADSB-SETUP wifi network the board broadcasts
3. browse to 192.168.4.1/setup and enter your own 2.4 GHz wifi creds
4. read the board's new IP off the 0.96" OLED
5. open that IP from any machine on the same network

Once it's on your LAN, check the receiver diagnostics page before you trust anything. The defaults use the LF (sub-GHz) input. Frequency correction starts in Observe mode, where it measures drift without acting on it. Let it watch real traffic for a while, then flip it to Apply. Cheap crystals drift, and a receiver that's slightly off-frequency looks exactly like a receiver with a bad antenna. People burn hours swapping antennas to fix a calibration problem.

Use a real USB-C data cable. The charge-only cable in your drawer will flash nothing and tell you nothing about why.

The Filter You Have to Kill

Here's where the build stops being a firmware install and turns into a hardware mod.

The W12's sub-GHz path has a SAW filter, U12, marked 2J1, sitting between the antenna port and the radio. Its job is to pass the LoRa band and reject everything else. It does that job well, which is the problem, because "everything else" includes 1090 MHz.

The README's fix is surgical. Remove U12, then bridge pads 1 and 4 with an insulated jumper so the antenna feeds the radio directly, and keep the jumper clear of pads 2, 3 and 5. Then connect your antenna to the LF/sub-GHz port.

A few notes from the bench side of this:

  • Use a fine tip or hot air. SAW filter packages are small and the pads lift if you get impatient. A tweezer-tip iron or a hot air station on low airflow is the civilized route.
  • Thin wire, short run. A short length of 30 AWG Kynar wire is ideal. At a gigahertz, a long loop of jumper is a tiny antenna of its own.
  • This is a one-way trip. Once U12 is gone, the LF path is unfiltered. LoRa use on that port gets noisier, and you're exposed to strong out-of-band signals that the filter used to eat. Treat the board as an ADS-B receiver from here on.

You can skip the mod. The HF/2.4 GHz input works without it. In the builder's testing, though, range was noticeably shorter on the unmodified path. The difference between 40 miles and 150 miles is one tiny filter and five minutes with a soldering iron.

Antennas, and the Wrong One That Works

The headline range came from an indoor 915 MHz antenna, the one cut for LoRa. That works because a 915 MHz whip is close enough to 1090 to resonate badly but usefully, and because airplanes are loud and high with nothing in the way.

You can do better for the price of a coffee. Wavelength at 1090 MHz is about 275 mm, so a quarter-wave element is about 69 mm. A quarter-wave ground plane (one 69 mm vertical element, four radials drooping at 45 degrees, all soldered to an SMA bulkhead connector) is a classic first antenna build for ADS-B, and it routinely beats store-bought whips. If you'd rather buy one, get something actually labeled for 1090 MHz with a 50 ohm feed.

Placement beats gain. Line of sight decides everything at this frequency. A cheap antenna in a top-floor window will outperform an expensive one on a desk surrounded by drywall, wiring and a monitor that leaks RF from every seam.

The optional GNSS module earns its slot here too. When the board knows where it is, range and bearing calculations make sense, and your track list stops being a list of numbers.

What You Give Up

This is a beautiful hack and an incomplete tool. Know the trade before you sell off your dongle.

A conventional RTL-SDR station, something like an RTL-SDR Blog V4 [AFFILIATE: RTL-SDR Blog V4] feeding readsb on a Pi, gives you a few things the W12 doesn't:

  • MLAT. Multilateration locates aircraft that broadcast Mode S without position data by comparing arrival times across many receivers. That needs precise timestamps and a feeder network. The W12 is on its own.
  • Feeding aggregators. The big community tracking networks expect standard decoder output. A custom ESP32 web page doesn't plug in without extra work.
  • Everything else on the spectrum. An SDR is a general-purpose radio. Tomorrow it can be an AIS receiver, a weather satellite station or a pager decoder. The W12 does one thing.

What you get in exchange is a receiver that boots in seconds, sips power from a USB brick, has no SD card to corrupt and no OS to patch, and costs less than a decent dinner. As a permanent window-sill sensor, a field unit in a go-bag, or a second station somewhere you'd never park a Pi, that trade is easy to justify.

The project also has honest edges. It's experimental. It's not an official Meshnology or Semtech product. A commenter on the Hackaday piece reported the W12 is hard to find in the US and EU outside Amazon India. Check availability before you plan a weekend around it.

Plaintext Sky

Back to that missing signature.

ADS-B is a protocol that announces everything and authenticates nothing. That makes it great for hobbyists and quietly uncomfortable for everyone else. Every aircraft with a working transponder broadcasts a permanent 24-bit address. The address maps to a registration. The registration maps to an owner. Log it for a month from one window and you have a pattern of life: who flies, when, where they go and how often they come back.

That's the OSINT angle, and it's why aircraft tracking keeps turning up in investigative work. Corporate jets telegraph acquisitions. Government flights telegraph visits. Private planes telegraph exactly what their owners would prefer they didn't. A $50 receiver that logs every ICAO address it hears is a surprisingly sharp instrument once you start keeping notes. If you go that route, a structured intel log matters more than the radio does. The template set in Obsidian + Claude Daily Ops (numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/obsidian-claude) was built for exactly this kind of recon-notebook habit, where raw captures become something you can actually search six weeks later.

The same plaintext design that makes listening easy makes injection theoretically easy, and that's been a research topic for over a decade: ghost aircraft, spoofed positions, the lot. Leave it on the page. Receiving 1090 MHz is legal in most places. Transmitting on it is the kind of mistake that ends with very serious people at your door, because you'd be interfering with live air traffic safety systems. The W12's radio can transmit. Don't let it near 1090 on the way out.

Defenders have the mirror-image problem: a receiver network that trusts plaintext can be fooled. Plausibility checks, multilateration and cross-referencing against primary radar are how serious systems cope. A single-board receiver like this one makes a nice teaching tool for that conversation, because it shows you exactly how little stands between the sky and your screen.

Where to Take It

Build one, mod the filter, cut a 69 mm ground plane, stick it in the highest window you have, and let it run for a week. Then point something at the data. Log every ICAO address to a file, count unique aircraft per hour, and flag any address you've seen more than ten times. Within a few days you'll know which tail numbers own your sky.

If this build hit the part of your brain that likes turning cheap ESP32 boards into field sensors, the rest of that playbook lives in Hardware Hacking for OSINT: Raspberry Pi War-Driving Box (numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/pidriver). It's the long-form version of this post's instincts: RF capture, firmware, and turning passive collection into intelligence without paying anyone a subscription.

The datasheet said 960. The airplanes said 1090. The airplanes were right.

Sources: Hackaday, "Building An ADS-B Receiver For Less Than You Think" (Nov 1, 2026); github.com/thefatmoop/esp32s3-lr2021-adsb-receiver; CNX Software on the Semtech LR2021; Strohmeier, Lenders and Martinovic, "On the Security of the Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast Protocol" (arXiv:1307.3664).

articles.title: Use it, or lose it 🧠
articles.description: Fayaz reminds everyone why we should keep doing deep intellectual and creative works.
articles.body_html:
Don't quit doing deep intellectual and creative work (like programming, art etc.) just because an LLM can do it well enough.

Even if an LLM can do your work perfectly for free (they can't do it perfectly yet, certainly not for free), you should keep doing some form of deep intellectual and creative work:

  1. To keep yourself intellectually healthy (like people do Gym Workout).
  2. To keep your agency (freedom, independence, authority, rights).

Again: use it, or lose it. 🧠✊😎✌️🫵

Fayaz

A Software Engineer who strongly believes you can add immense value by knowingly implementing Software Engineering best practices even at the age of AI, and puts human life and dignity above all else.

articles.title: Product Hunt Launches Look Impressive. But Do They Bring Paying Customers?
articles.description: TL;DR   Public founder accounts of Product Hunt launches swing from zero paying customers to...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • Public founder accounts of Product Hunt launches swing from zero paying customers to hundreds. Anyone quoting you a clean "average conversion rate" is guessing.
  • The only large dataset I found ties launches to Series A funding, not to revenue, and even that link is modest.
  • A launch is a one-day discovery channel. It turns into a customer strategy only when you add targeting and follow-up.
  • Don't judge a launch by its rank. Judge it with a scorecard you write before launch day. There's one at the bottom.

One of the most useful Product Hunt write-ups I've read has no victory lap in it. A founder launched BrandingStudio.ai and finished the day at #6 with 168 upvotes. Four days later he wrote up the aftermath: more than 400 signups, 360 brands created, and $237 in total revenue, all from a single paying customer.

He did the math himself. That's a 0.25 percent conversion rate. His conclusion was refreshingly sober: people were curious enough to try the product, but not sure enough to pay for it.

Most launch screenshots stop at the rank. This one kept going, and the second half is where the interesting stuff is.

So here's the question I want to dig into. Does a Product Hunt launch help startups find paying customers, or does it mostly hand you a day of attention that looks like traction? I can't give you a universal answer, and by the end you'll see why nobody can. What I can do is show what the public evidence supports, where it runs out, and how to judge your own launch by what it did for the business instead of where it landed on a leaderboard.

First, a word on where the numbers come from

I sorted everything I used into four buckets: firsthand founder accounts (self-reported, nobody audited them), third-party compilations, published research, and my own analysis. Hypothetical examples are labeled as hypothetical. And when a company never shared its revenue or customer numbers, I say so instead of filling the gap with a guess.

Keep that in mind as we go. Most of what follows is founders telling their own stories, and founders are human.

Why everyone wants the badge

Product Hunt's own launch guide pitches the site as a place to build momentum and reach your first wave of users. It points at Loom, Cursor and Clubhouse as products that used it as a launch pad. Launches go live at 12:01 AM Pacific on the scheduled day, and the guide says you can launch again when you ship a major update.

And honestly, that's useful for a small team. A launch is a dated, public event with a leaderboard attached. It gives you a deadline, a reason to finish the thing, a link to send around, and a badge for your homepage.

The catch: you can collect every one of those benefits without a single person paying you. That's why I like to keep them in a separate pile from what most founders say they actually want, which is customers.

What the leaderboard is really measuring

Product Hunt doesn't publish its ranking formula. Its CTO has said in a community post that launches are ranked by points rather than raw upvotes, that votes from verified users tend to carry more weight, and that a launch with strong evidence of paid votes gets un-featured. A third-party summary of the help center describes points as a blend of upvotes and meaningful engagement, and says the official advice is not to ask people outright for upvotes.

The homepage is curated by humans. According to the featuring guidelines as summarized by Syften, editors look for live products that are useful, novel, well made or creative. Some formats, like waitlist-only launches, lists, templates and courses, don't get featured on the homepage. These rules change, so read the current versions before you plan around them.

Here's my own reading of all this, and it's an opinion, not a fact from any source. A rank measures how many of the right accounts engaged with your launch during one day, compared with everyone else who launched that day. Product appeal matters. So do your existing network, your timing and your competition. None of those is the same thing as someone wanting to buy.

There's also the price of getting there. In a small roundup of May 2026 launches, the three founders who reported prep time put it at roughly 40 to 65 hours, and a few said they were awake for 20 to 24 hours on launch day. One of them warned that asking friends and family to vote can backfire, because a lot of them don't have accounts, and freshly created ones may not count.

To be clear, nothing in these accounts shows founders neglecting their product to chase votes, and I'm not accusing anyone of gaming anything. The narrower point is just that a launch eats a lot of hours, and every hour spent rounding up supporters is an hour you're not spending talking to potential customers.

What founders actually report

The public record is a scattering of self-reported stories. Here are the ones I found, with the source type noted, because it matters.

Launch What the founder reported Source type
BrandingStudio.ai #6 of the day, 168 upvotes. After four days: 400+ signups, 360 brands created, 1 paying customer, $237 revenue Founder post, Indie Hackers
Roly AI #13, 110 upvotes. After three days: 323 site visitors, 26 signups, 0 paying customers Founder post, Product Hunt forum
Website Rooms Fewer than 20 upvotes, a few signups, 0 paid users Founder newsletter
Buttondown Front page of Product Hunt and Hacker News. About 30,000 unique visitors, about 500 registered users, maybe 10 paying customers Founder interview, Starter Story
Stock Market GPT 69 upvotes, 4 sales (revenue not stated) Founder post, Indie Hackers
gptengineer.app 500k+ impressions, 16k signups, 850 paying users (5 percent), from launches plus Hacker News and Twitter posts Founder write-up, Product Hunt
Reply.io About 10,000 visitors in two days, 600 signups, about 60 paying customers Founder statement compiled by Founderpath (secondary)

Read them side by side and a few things jump out.

The range is huge. The same platform gave some founders zero paying customers and another one hundreds. The products, prices, audiences and surrounding effort are so different that the platform can't be the main explanation. That's the first honest conclusion I can offer: Product Hunt is a venue, and venues don't produce uniform results.

The funnel ratios are all over the place. From the figures above, Buttondown's founder saw roughly 1.7 percent of unique visitors become registered users (500 of 30,000), and about 2 percent of those become paying customers. Roly AI saw about 8 percent of visitors sign up (26 of 323). Reply.io's numbers work out to around 6 percent of visitors signing up and 10 percent of signups paying, while gptengineer reports 5 percent of signups paying.

But the products, prices and even the definition of "signup" differ, so none of these is a benchmark. The spread itself is the lesson. If you see a confident "average Product Hunt conversion rate" somewhere, ask where it came from.

The spike fades fast. Roly AI's founder logged 229 visitors on day one (68 of them from Product Hunt), 64 on day two (20 from Product Hunt), and 33 on day three (none from Product Hunt). That's one small product with no existing audience, but it lines up with how Buttondown's founder is described in the Founderpath compilation, which mentions a very prominent spike in the signup graph.

The good outcomes are real, and they're messier than the rank. gptengineer has the best numbers in the table. But the write-up says the launch only went from flailing to successful after some mid-day decisions: dropping the waitlist, posting on Hacker News, and shortening the launch post for Twitter. The founder also says the user interviews after launch were the most valuable part. Founderpath's compilation lists several other founders who credit a launch for their first customers.

Did the launch cause those customers, or did it just happen to coincide with founders who were doing a lot of other things right? None of these accounts can settle that.

The sample is biased both ways. Founders publish their best and their worst results, and compilations with titles like "29 strategies" lean toward success stories. Nobody has sampled all launches, so the share of launches that end in revenue is simply unknown. If someone hands you that number with a straight face, they're quoting a tiny sample or making it up.

One more data point deserves its own paragraph. In that May 2026 roundup, a software vendor asked five founders the same questions and published results for four of them. It's self-reported, tiny, and the author calls the figures directional. Still, all four launches finished in the top six that day. The highest-ranked one reported 0 percent paid conversion so far (usage-based pricing, early days), while a launch in the middle of the pack reported around 20 percent of signups paying.

That founder's explanation was about the audience. The product serves founders who are actively raising money, and they tend to convert 7 to 10 days after signing up. Four launches prove nothing statistically. But they show how a rank and a revenue number can drift apart, and why the window you measure over matters.

The one big dataset, and what it can't tell you

The only large-scale analysis I found that links Product Hunt launches to a business outcome is about funding, not sales. A preprint (not peer reviewed, as far as I can tell) matched 67,292 featured launches from 2019 to 2025 against Crunchbase records. It found 528 that announced a Series A within 18 months, which is 0.78 percent. Launches that did tended to have more upvotes, better daily ranks, bigger maker teams and B2B topics. A #1 daily rank went with a 2.22 percent rate, compared with 0.51 percent for launches ranked 11th or lower.

So rank does carry a little information about later funding. But four limits stop me from turning that into advice.

  1. Funding isn't revenue. The paper says nothing about paying customers.
  2. It's an association. The authors' own reading is that the strongest signals combine team size with votes, which hints that the launch mostly records how well-connected a team already was. My take is that a launch may reflect strength more than it creates it, though the data can't separate the two.
  3. Crunchbase covers US, institutionally backed companies better than bootstrapped or international ones. So the dataset is thinnest exactly where a lot of indie founders live.
  4. The predictive power is modest. The authors' best model, tested on held-out data, was about 4.7 times better than chance on a base rate under 1 percent. That still leaves most of its picks wrong.

"The launch went well" is hiding a whole funnel

When a founder says the launch went well, they usually mean something from the very top of a long chain. It helps to name every link, because each one breaks for a different reason.

Stage The question it answers Where you see it
Impressions and visibility Did people see the listing? Product Hunt page, impressions
Visitors Did they click through? Your analytics
Signups Did anyone raise a hand? Your database
Activated users Did they reach a first useful result? Product events
Returning users Did they come back? Day 7 and day 30 cohorts
Free-to-paid conversion Did someone decide it was worth money? Billing
Paying customers Who, and at what price? Billing and CRM
Retained, profitable customers Do they stay, and do they cost less to serve than they pay? Cohort revenue against cost

Upvotes live outside this chain entirely. They're a social signal about the listing, and they can go up while nothing downstream moves.

BrandingStudio is a good example of why the stages matter. By the founder's own count, nearly every signup went on to create a brand, so activation was strong. Payment is where the chain snapped. His diagnosis was a gap between "this looks useful" and "I know exactly what to do next." That's a pricing and offer problem, not a traffic problem.

A founder who only watched signups would have thrown a party. A founder who only watched revenue wouldn't have known where to look. The stage where people drop out tells you what to fix.

Why launches sometimes don't turn into customers

These reasons come from individual accounts plus my own analysis, and none of them applies to every product.

Curiosity can outnumber intent. People on Product Hunt are browsing a feed of new things. If your product is something people only need when a specific problem hits, browsers may sign up and drift off, or convert days later like the founder in the roundup described. I couldn't find any public data on what share of Product Hunt visitors match a particular buyer profile, so test it yourself: compare your signups against the customer you described before launch.

The audience you bring can matter more than the platform. In the roundup, signup counts ranged from 71 to roughly 450, and the highest figure bundled Product Hunt together with LinkedIn activity the founder had built around the launch. The founders pointed to owned audiences, like email lists and networks, as the thing they'd keep. If you have none, a launch has less to amplify.

Value that takes effort to see. If your product needs setup before it shows its worth, launch-day visitors may leave before they find out. If it works inside a minute, a high-traffic day suits it much better.

Distribution as an afterthought. The Website Rooms founder wrote that he spent three weeks building and one day preparing distribution, and decided he'd fallen into the trap of treating "distribution" as "launch on Product Hunt and Hacker News." That's a planning lesson. It says nothing bad about the platform.

No follow-up. A day-three traffic number near zero is normal. What you can still recover are the people who signed up. The founders who reported real value, like gptengineer's, point to conversations after launch day.

Two made-up startups, to make this concrete

Startup A and Startup B below are invented for illustration. Their numbers aren't benchmarks and don't describe any real company.

Startup A sells a general productivity tool at $12 a month. It finishes second for the day with 1,100 upvotes. Nine thousand people visit, 700 sign up, 85 reach the first useful result, and 6 start paying. By day 60, two of the six have cancelled, which leaves $48 in monthly revenue. The founder's follow-up emails to the people who never activated get almost no replies, because most of them were just curious and never had the problem the product solves.

Startup B sells a $49 monthly tool for one narrow job: reconciling payouts for small online shops. It finishes ninth with 90 upvotes. Six hundred people visit, 45 sign up, and 20 reach the first useful result (the signup form asked which platform they use, and onboarding was built around the answer). Five start paying. At day 60, four are still around, which is $196 a month. The founder has also talked to a dozen shop owners and knows three features they'd pay for.

On the leaderboard, A wins by a mile. On revenue, retention and learning, B is ahead, and B's next ten customers will probably look a lot like its first five.

This isn't a rule that small launches beat big ones. If A tightened its positioning and fixed onboarding, its bigger funnel could easily overtake B. The point is that the leaderboard can't tell you which situation you're in. Only the later stages of the funnel can.

Where Product Hunt genuinely helps

Several benefits show up across the accounts above, and they deserve to be taken seriously.

  • First stranger traffic. Roly AI launched with no social media presence and still got 68 visits from the site on day one. It's modest, but it's more than zero, and zero is where most products start.
  • Feedback and positioning lessons. gptengineer's founder valued the post-launch interviews most. The Stock Market GPT founder reports making four sales and learning more about what customers wanted.
  • Early adopters. Buttondown's founder reported around ten paying customers from a launch that, by his own description, wasn't meteoric. For an early product, that first handful can be exactly what's needed.
  • Conversations. In the May 2026 roundup, two of five founders reported unprompted investor interest, and another reactivated some cold leads.
  • Second chances. The official guide encourages launching again when you ship something significant, so a quiet first launch doesn't close the door.

The distinction I keep coming back to is discovery channel versus customer acquisition strategy. A discovery channel puts your product in front of people for a day. A strategy includes who you're trying to reach, what you want them to do, how you'll follow up, and what happens next. Product Hunt can be the first. It doesn't hand you the second.

When a launch probably isn't your next move

A launch tends to be the wrong step in a few situations:

  • Nobody has told you they'd pay. A launch won't fix that, and visitors who politely click around can hide it. Talk to ten people who have the problem first.
  • Your buyers are a short list you can name. Think heads of operations at regional logistics firms. Direct outreach will teach you more per hour than a public leaderboard.
  • The product can't be tried today. The featuring guidelines I mentioned earlier leave waitlist-only launches off the homepage, so you'd be preparing for a launch that can't get its best exposure.
  • You have no way to follow up. Launch traffic evaporates. The only durable thing you keep is whatever you captured: an email, a conversation, a note about what someone tried to do.
  • The real bottleneck is something else. If it's pricing, onboarding or positioning, extra traffic just makes the problem more expensive to observe.

What to try instead, or alongside

None of this replaces Product Hunt in general. Each option wins under particular conditions, and this whole section is my analysis, not research.

Direct outreach makes sense when you can name your buyers and find them. A founder selling to small accounting firms can email fifty of them this week, and each reply will probably teach more than a hundred upvotes. Relevant communities work when you already take part in them, and they flop when you only show up to announce something. Founder-led content suits products with a point of view and compounds slowly. Search-intent content fits problems people already google, but its slow payoff makes it a poor stand-in if you need a signal this month. Partnerships make sense when another product's users hit your problem right after using theirs. Referrals need customers first, which is a good reason to find your first ones another way.

Whichever you pick, run it as a small experiment: one channel, a time limit, one number to beat.

A scorecard for deciding whether your launch worked

This is a framework I put together for this article. It isn't an established model, and it has no universal thresholds. Every target in it is yours, and you set it before launch day.

Before launch

  • Is the product ready for real users? A stranger should be able to sign up and reach a first useful result without your help. Watch three people you don't know try it. Make the price visible.
  • Who exactly should find it? Write the buyer in one sentence: role, situation, the problem in their words. Then ask whether those people actually browse Product Hunt. If you can't answer, that's a finding.
  • What specific outcome do you want? Pick one primary outcome and put a number on it, like ten activated users who match your buyer profile, five booked customer conversations, or three paying customers. Upvotes can be a side note.
  • How will you measure beyond upvotes? Define the activation event (the first useful thing a user does), tag Product Hunt traffic with its own source parameter, and record your baseline.
  • Can you follow up? Have a welcome email ready, a way to reach people who didn't activate, and a link for booking a call.

During the launch

  • What to track: visitors by source, signups, activation events, and the questions people ask. Sort comments into use questions, objections, feature requests and plain praise.
  • How to collect feedback: answer every comment, and add one open question to the signup or welcome email, like what the person hoped to do.
  • Real interest or casual curiosity? Look for signups who match your buyer profile, activate within a day, reply to your welcome email, or ask about pricing. Curiosity tends to leave no trace after the click.
  • Learning from people who don't sign up: check where they leave, how many viewed pricing, and, if you have the tools, watch session recordings. A short on-site question can explain a lot.

After the launch

At day 7, fill in the scorecard below with your real numbers, then reach out to every activated user and every high-fit signup who didn't activate. At day 30, check who came back, who paid, which conversations are still alive, and how many hours the whole thing cost you.

Measure What to record Your target Day 7 Day 30
Fit Share of signups matching your buyer profile
Activation Share reaching the first useful result
Return Users active again after a week, after a month
Revenue signal Paying customers, plus qualified conversations
Learning Feedback that changed a decision
Cost Hours spent on prep, launch day and follow-up

Then read the card by where it breaks:

  • Low fit means you attracted the wrong audience. Change who you aim at before you touch the product.
  • Good fit but low activation points at onboarding or positioning.
  • Good activation but little return points at value.
  • Return without payment points at pricing or the offer. That was the BrandingStudio pattern.
  • Fit, activation and return all healthy but volume small? Distribution is your constraint, and relaunching with a meaningful update is a reasonable experiment.

What would justify spending more time on this channel? Your own pre-written targets getting met, with customers or serious conversations coming from people who match your buyer profile. A few paying users who fit and stay beat a giant pile of signups that never activate. And if the evidence isn't there, the next month is better spent talking to customers directly.

The decision underneath all of this

A leaderboard position is a fact about one day. A customer is a fact about your business. Product Hunt can help with the first and sometimes contributes to the second, and the evidence we have doesn't say how often.

What it does say is that a launch is a way to get attention, and a startup survives on what happens to that attention afterward.

So treat your launch as an experiment. Write down who you want to reach, what you want them to do, and what result would make you do it again. Then judge it by those answers, not by the badge.

I'd love to hear real numbers in the comments. If you've launched on Product Hunt, what did your day-7 and day-30 picture look like compared with your launch-day rank? Failures count too, and they're usually the more useful ones.

articles.title: My 'Second Backend' Existed Only in the README
articles.description: The release gate said "two OTel backends proven." The check proving it ended in || true.  It had been...
articles.body_html:
The release gate said "two OTel backends proven." The check proving it ended in || true.

It had been passing for weeks. Against a service that was never started, never configured, and never received a single span.

This is from the agentwatch v0.2.1 release — the agent-security tool in agentic-suite. The full forensics are in the v0.2.0 field test report.

The claim and the check

agentwatch emits OpenTelemetry GenAI spans. The release gate for v0.2.0 has an expanded item, number 10:

Two OTel backends proven — an agent-span tree must render in Jaeger and Tempo, not just whichever backend happened to be wired up first.

The field-test case behind it, FT-BACKEND-2, checked the Tempo side. Its assertion was, in essence:

curl -sf http://localhost:3200/api/search/tags || true

Port 3200 is Tempo's search API. The curl asks "is Tempo up and does it answer?" And then || true answers the question permanently: yes, whatever curl said.

That's a check that cannot fail. It's also a check someone wrote with good intentions — the || true is there so the case doesn't hard-fail on a flaky timing window. It's defensive shell. And it converted a release-gate claim into a string in a script.

What was actually running

The stack definition (lib.sh) listed the v0.2.0 profile services. Tempo wasn't among them. The collector config (deploy/otel-collector-config.yml) had one exporter: otlp/jaeger.

So the topology behind the "two backends" claim was:

Claimed Actually
Jaeger receiving spans ✅ up, receiving
Tempo receiving spans ❌ never started, never configured, no exporter pointing at it
Field-test status PASS

The check passed because the check was unpassable. Not because the system worked.

The part I like: hardening made it fail

Here's where the story turns. The v0.2.0 field test had 94 cases, and after the run I did a hardening pass — going case by case, asking of each assertion: could this fail if the claim were false?

FT-BACKEND-2 couldn't. So the || true came out, and the check became a real query: Tempo's search API must answer for the service agentwatch emits as.

Then the case ran red. And the red was not a test bug. The red was the finding.

That inversion took me a while to appreciate. We're trained to treat a red field test as "the test is broken until proven otherwise." But a check that can fail, failing, is the system telling you something a green check never will. The report we published says it plainly: the old || true hid that the R4 claim was unmet. The green wasn't evidence. It was upholstery.

The fix was three lines of infrastructure

Not a test fix — an actual product fix:

  1. tempo added to the profile services (and a tempo-config.yml to match).
  2. A new otlp/tempo exporter in the collector config, added to the fan-out list.
  3. The sibling case (FT-OTEL-1) hardened too — it now asserts a real parent/child agent-span tree renders, a CHILD_OF relationship, in Jaeger and Tempo, rather than grepping a service name out of one backend's API.

Re-run: the stack comes up 16 services including svc-tempo, the trace resolves in Tempo, and both cases pass — now for reasons. The v0.2.1 release gate table reads gate 10 as PASS (fixed) with the Tempo receipt attached.

The class of bug, generalized

|| true is the obvious member. But the same genus showed up all over the census we did of the 94 field-test assertions:

Shape Looks like Can fail when claim is false?
`\ \ true`
test -f <path> "artifact exists" Only if packaging breaks entirely
python -c "import x" "module ships" Only if the import system itself fails
grep -q <word> on your own output "feature works" Only if the word stops appearing
Driver runs, prints ok: ... "scenario passed" Only if the driver exits non-zero

We tallied it: across 94 cases, 52 were driver-run, 11 existence/syntax, 9 substring-greps, 5 module-imports, 1 outright || true — and only about 8 asserted a real condition. That's the sentence I'd want on a wall somewhere: most of your green is plumbing, and plumbing can't fail.

The v0.2.0 campaign grounded 90 of 92 passing cases on checks that can fail. That's the actual product of that release, more than any feature.

What I keep from this

  • A check that cannot fail is not a check. It's documentation with an exit code.
  • || true on a probe is fine (you don't want probes failing your build). || true on a gate is a lie with good intentions.
  • When a hardened assertion goes red, the first hypothesis should shift over time: early in a project it's "test wrong," late in a project it's "system wrong." This one was late.
  • Release-gate claims need an assertion per claim, not an assertion per area. "Backends" isn't a claim. "Jaeger and Tempo each render the tree" is.

All of it shipped in agentwatch v0.2.1 — on PyPI.

The question worth asking of your own release gates: for each one, what's the check, and could that check fail tomorrow if the claim stopped being true? If any answer is "no," you've found the next field test.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.2.1 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • v0.2.0 field test report — FT-BACKEND-2 (R4), the || true finding, and the assertion-shape census
  • The collector config, fixed — otlp/tempo exporter + fan-out
  • The release checklist, gate 10
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools

articles.title: Cell Towers Are Optional: At 16, I Built a Hybrid 800m Off-Grid Mesh Protocol for Smartphones (No LoRa Required)
articles.description: How I combined BLE, Wi-Fi Direct, UWB, and Delay-Tolerant Networking into AirPin — a zero-server P2P...
articles.body_html:
How I combined BLE, Wi-Fi Direct, UWB, and Delay-Tolerant Networking into AirPin — a zero-server P2P engine that turns regular phones into an encrypted relay network.

What happens when cell towers go down, Wi-Fi is dead, or you are deep in the wilderness—and you don't have specialized LoRa hardware like a Meshtastic node in your backpack?

Every modern smartphone already carries a ridiculous amount of radio silicon: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Wi-Fi Direct, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). Yet almost every off-grid messenger on the market locks itself into a single transport layer (usually BLE), suffering from terrible bandwidth, short range, or rapid battery drain.

Over the past year, I decided to fix this. I designed and built AirPin—a hybrid, multi-protocol P2P mesh routing engine that dynamically switches between radio interfaces and uses Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) to bounce encrypted messages from phone to phone without the internet or central servers. It serves as the core engine of my upcoming super-app ecosystem, Prux.

Here is the story and technical breakdown of how AirPin works under the hood, how multi-hop relay behaves in real-world field tests, and the architectural problems I had to solve along the way.

Why Single-Radio Offline Messengers Fail

If you look at classic off-grid apps like Bridgefy or Briar, they hit a hard physics wall:

  • BLE-only mesh: Great for background discovery and low battery usage, but throughput is tiny, and real-world range drops sharply in dense environments.
  • Wi-Fi Direct: High bandwidth and up to 200+ meters line-of-sight range, but keeping Wi-Fi Direct awake 24/7 destroys smartphone batteries and triggers aggressive OS background killers on iOS and Android.

Instead of choosing one radio, I built AirPin as a dynamic link-layer router that treats BLE, UWB, and Wi-Fi Direct as a single adaptive pipeline.

Inside the AirPin 4-Layer Stack

AirPin operates automatically in the background across four distinct stages, choosing the right radio for the right moment:

  1. Always-On Discovery: Devices running Prux broadcast lightweight, rotating cryptographic beacons over Bluetooth Low Energy. Because BLE uses almost zero power, it acts as a silent radar. Short text messages and initial handshakes go straight through BLE without waking heavier radios.
  2. Spatial Ranging & Direction (UWB): When supported by the phone's hardware, Ultra-Wideband gives centimeter-accurate distance and directional vectors between peers. Instead of blindly flooding packets to every phone nearby, AirPin knows which nodes are physically moving toward the destination or holding the strongest link.
  3. High-Speed Burst Escalation (Wi-Fi Direct): When you send voice notes, images, or need maximum single-hop distance (up to 200+ meters in open terrain), AirPin negotiates a handshake over BLE, spins up a temporary Wi-Fi Direct P2P tunnel for a few seconds, blasts the encrypted payload across, and immediately puts the high-power radio back to sleep.
  4. Store-and-Forward Relay (DTN): What if there is no continuous chain of users between you and your friend right now? AirPin uses Delay-Tolerant Networking. A message hops across intermediate phones like a baton in a relay race (reaching 750–800 meters across 4 hops in field tests). If the chain breaks, an intermediate phone securely caches the encrypted packet in an isolated sandbox and forwards it minutes later when it walks past another user.

Zero-Server Security: Can Strangers Read My Relayed Messages?

Bouncing your private messages through strangers' phones sounds terrifying at first. To make it bulletproof, AirPin enforces strict cryptographic isolation:

  • End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) at the Edge: Messages are encrypted on the sender's device before they ever touch the AirPin router. Intermediate relay phones only see an opaque encrypted envelope, a randomized packet hash (to prevent infinite broadcast loops), and a hop counter (TTL).
  • Zero Cloud Storage: Off-grid messages never touch a central server. Even when Prux operates in standard online mode, message history stays strictly on user devices.
  • SunFlower Visual Codes: You can't trust a central key server when you are offline. I created custom visual SunFlower codes (a specialized alternative to standard QR codes) so users can verify identities and exchange encryption keys face-to-face in a split second.

Real-World Field Tests & Recognition from Chipmakers

Testing a mesh protocol in an IDE simulator is easy; testing it in the real world is brutal. I live on the Pacific coast of the Russian Far East, surrounded by steep hills, dense taiga, and coastline where dead cellular zones are an everyday reality.

In field tests across urban and open terrain, AirPin achieved:

  • 40–80 meters single-hop range indoors and in dense city blocks.
  • 200+ meters single-hop range in open line-of-sight.
  • 750–800 meters end-to-end delivery across a 4-hop chain of smartphones without internet or cell service.

Earlier this year, I pitched and defended the AirPin architecture in English at the 40th CASTIC international science and engineering competition in China. Out of 600+ projects, AirPin placed in the Top 20 and won the Unisoc Innovation Award directly from UNISOC, one of the world's largest mobile processor and baseband chipmakers. The technology is also officially registered with Rospatent (Software Reg. #2026607225, Patent Pending #2026112785).

Why I Wrapped a Mesh Protocol Inside a "Liquid Glass" Super-App

Here is the dirty secret of every standalone offline messenger: nobody has it installed when an emergency actually happens. People delete single-purpose emergency apps because they don't use them on a normal Tuesday.

To make a smartphone mesh network work in the real world, you need node density—people actually keeping the app on their phones every day. That is why I built Prux around AirPin, featuring a custom "Liquid Glass" UI for iOS, Android, and macOS. Alongside the off-grid messenger, Prux includes daily-driver mini-apps:

  • Prux Mail: Built-in email client aggregating multiple accounts in one clean inbox.
  • Loud Music: Offline-capable music player.

  • ZheykPay: Integrated crypto wallet.

  • Red Panda & Mahjong Blast: Language learning tools and mini-games.

The more people use Prux for music, mail, or everyday chatting, the stronger and wider the invisible AirPin mesh network becomes whenever the grid goes down.

Follow the Build & Join the Beta

I am currently running closed beta tests and fine-tuning background BLE/Wi-Fi Direct wake-locks ahead of the public launch in Spring 2027.

I'm building Prux and AirPin in public and sharing raw engineering logs, range test videos, and UI previews over on X. If you love mesh networking, P2P protocols, or mobile systems engineering, come say hi and follow the journey:

  • Follow me on X (Twitter) for live dev updates: https://x.com/Prux_Messenger
  • Telegram Channel: https://t.me/Prux_channel
  • Official Website: https://www.prux.su

Questions for the devs here:

  • Would you be interested in an open standalone SDK for AirPin so you could drop offline mesh messaging into your own mobile apps?

articles.title: Locus Earth: Building an Open-Source 3D Globe That Runs Directly in Your Browser 🌍
articles.description: Have you ever wanted to explore the Earth in 3D without installing a dedicated desktop...
articles.body_html:
Have you ever wanted to explore the Earth in 3D without installing a dedicated desktop application?

That's exactly what I wanted to build.

Locus Earth is an open-source, browser-based 3D globe application inspired by Google Earth. It combines interactive 3D terrain, satellite imagery, 3D buildings, measurement tools, location search, and more — all accessible directly from a modern web browser.

No complicated installation. No account registration. Just open the page and start exploring.

But this project is about more than displaying a 3D globe. I wanted to build something that feels like a complete mapping application, works across desktop and mobile devices, and remains relatively easy for other developers to explore and modify.

Let's take a look!

🌍 What is Locus Earth?

Locus Earth is built with CesiumJS, an open-source JavaScript library for 3D geospatial visualization.

The application provides an interactive virtual globe with:

  • Global satellite imagery and 3D terrain.
  • Global 3D buildings based on OpenStreetMap data.
  • Multiple imagery providers and map styles.
  • Location search and navigation.
  • Distance and area measurement.
  • Custom markers, paths, and polygons.
  • Day/night lighting simulation.
  • Dark and light themes.
  • Offline imagery caching.
  • Progressive Web App (PWA) support.

The interface is designed for both desktop and mobile devices, with touch-friendly controls and an adaptive layout.

🗺️ Exploring the World

One of the main features is the ability to switch between different imagery sources.

Instead of relying on a single basemap, Locus Earth integrates several providers:

  • Sentinel-2
  • Blue Marble
  • Nighttime satellite imagery
  • Tianditu satellite imagery
  • Tencent Maps

This gives users different ways to explore the same location.

The application also supports terrain visualization and 3D buildings, making the experience more immersive than a traditional flat map.

Region-aware features

Some features are activated depending on the geographic area being viewed.

For example:

  • In supported cities such as Denver, Washington, D.C., and Sydney, the application automatically switches to higher-detail city models.
  • When browsing mainland China, a Street View button becomes available, allowing users to jump to panoramic imagery.

There is also an experimental Google 3D mode that uses a Google 3D Tiles demonstration asset hosted on Cesium ion. Its availability depends on network connectivity and the continued availability of that asset.

📐 More Than Just a Globe

I didn't want Locus Earth to be just something users open, look at, and close.

So I added several practical mapping tools.

Measurement tools

Users can measure distances and areas directly on the globe.

Both polylines and polygons follow the terrain rather than simply floating above the surface.

Completed measurements can also be named and saved for later use.

Markers, paths, and favorites

Users can create custom markers, paths, and geometric shapes.

These objects are organized in a unified favorites system and stored locally in the browser.

They can also be exported and imported using KML (XML), making it easier to preserve or transfer user-created geographic data.

Location search

Simply enter a place name to navigate to it.

The built-in geocoder makes it possible to jump between locations without manually navigating the globe.

🌗 A Few Details That Make It Feel Like an Application

There are also several smaller features that make everyday interaction more convenient:

  • Day/night simulation with adjustable time.
  • Sun and Moon lighting.
  • Optional 3D terrain.
  • Building model visibility controls.
  • Compass and camera tilt reset.
  • Draggable floating toolbar.
  • System-aware light and dark themes.

These features may seem relatively small individually, but together they help make the application feel more complete.

⚙️ The Technical Side: Why Zero Build?

One of my most important architectural decisions was to avoid a traditional build pipeline.

Locus Earth uses native JavaScript ES Modules.

There is no bundler, transpiler, or complicated compilation process required to run the application.

The project is essentially a static web application.

This approach has several advantages:

  • The source code can be inspected directly.
  • There is no build step before deployment.
  • Changes can be tested quickly.
  • Hosting is straightforward.
  • Contributors can work with the actual source files.

The application also uses a Service Worker and Web App Manifest to provide PWA functionality.

For deployment, it can be hosted on static hosting platforms such as GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages.

📱 Offline Support

Offline functionality was another feature I wanted to include.

Locus Earth supports local caching of imagery tiles.

Once an area has been visited and its imagery has been cached, users can revisit that area even without an active network connection.

However, offline functionality has limitations:

  • Previously cached imagery can still be displayed.
  • Terrain data still requires a network connection.
  • 3D buildings still require a network connection.
  • Location search still requires a network connection.

The goal isn't to turn the entire globe into a fully offline application, but to make previously explored areas more accessible.

📲 Bringing It to Android

Although Locus Earth is fundamentally a web application, I also wanted to provide an Android installation option.

Instead of rewriting the entire application in Kotlin or building a separate native mapping engine, I created a lightweight Android WebView wrapper.

The APK essentially opens the online application in a fullscreen native window.

It provides:

  • A fullscreen experience without a browser address bar.
  • Domain whitelisting.
  • External links opened in the system browser.
  • A simple first-launch explanation that the application is web-based.

And here's an interesting part:

The Android application does not contain the actual mapping logic.

The web application is still the main product, and its content is loaded online.

This means that when I update the website, existing Android installations automatically receive the updated version.

There is no need to rebuild or redistribute the APK for ordinary website updates.

The Android wrapper only needs to be rebuilt when its own configuration changes, such as the application icon, package name, or allowed domains.

The Android project is also included in the repository, so developers can build their own versions.

🤖 Built with AI Assistance

Locus Earth has been developed with assistance from several large language models.

The models used during development include:

  • DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
  • Hunyuan4
  • ChatGPT-4o

AI assistance has been part of the development process, helping with implementation, debugging, and exploring possible solutions.

However, the project still involves plenty of testing, integration, troubleshooting, and decisions about how different components should work together.

Getting individual features to work is one thing. Making them work together reliably across different browsers and devices is another challenge entirely.

🛠️ Technology Stack

Here's a quick overview:

Component| Technology
3D Globe Engine| CesiumJS 1.118.2
Architecture| Native JavaScript ES Modules
Rendering| WebGL 2
PWA| Service Worker + Web App Manifest
Android| Native Android WebView wrapper
Geographic Data| Cesium ion, OpenStreetMap, Natural Earth
Imagery Providers| Multiple map providers
Deployment| GitHub Pages / Cloudflare Pages

The entire project is released under the MIT License.

Both the web application and Android wrapper source code are available in the repository.

🚀 Try It Yourself!

You can access Locus Earth directly in your browser:

GitHub Pages:
https://zhunemo.github.io/locus-earth/

Cloudflare Pages:
https://locus-earth.pages.dev

Source Code:
https://github.com/ZhuNemo/locus-earth

For developers interested in contributing, modifying, or self-hosting the project, the repository also includes documentation covering development decisions, configuration, deployment, and Android APK builds.

One important note: the API keys included in the repository are restricted to the project's own domains. If you fork or deploy your own instance, you'll need to obtain and configure your own API keys.

Final Thoughts

Locus Earth started as a personal project, but it gradually grew into something much more substantial.

There were plenty of challenges along the way: rendering compatibility, mobile browser behavior, integrating different geographic data sources, caching strategies, and making the interface work well on different screen sizes.

It's still an independently maintained project, and there is always room for improvement.

For now, I'm happy with where it has arrived.

If you're interested in 3D maps, CesiumJS, geospatial visualization, or just want to explore an alternative browser-based globe, give it a try!

Happy exploring! 🌍

articles.title: I Deleted My Scroll-Lock Library's Ugly Hack. `scrollbar-gutter` Replaces It.
articles.description: Opening a modal shifts your whole page sideways because the scrollbar vanishes with it — the bug every scroll-lock library papers over with a JS width measurement and a padding-right hack. `scrollbar-gutter: stable` fixes it in one line now that Safari finally caught up.
articles.body_html:
You open a modal. For one frame, before you can even read what it says, the page behind it flinches — the whole column of text shifts a few pixels to the right, like the browser flinched too.

Close the modal and it snaps back. Nobody styled that. Nobody asked for it. And if you build UI on Windows or Linux, you've shipped it to production without noticing, because on a Mac with the default trackpad scrollbars, it's nearly invisible. That's the part that makes this bug so sticky: the person who can see it and the person who has to fix it are usually not using the same operating system.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The standard explanation is that overflow: hidden on <body> — the thing every modal, drawer, and dropdown uses to stop the page scrolling behind it — also removes the vertical scrollbar. Removing the scrollbar hands its width back to the content. The content reflows into that space. The page shifts.

So people fix it the only way CSS used to allow: measure the scrollbar, then pay it back in padding.

function lockScroll() {
  const scrollbarWidth = window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth;
  document.body.style.paddingRight = `${scrollbarWidth}px`;
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden";
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.paddingRight = "";
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

This works. It's also the entire reason body-scroll-lock, react-remove-scroll, and half a dozen modal libraries ship their own copy of this exact measurement. Every one of them is solving the same problem: find out how wide the scrollbar would have been, then fake its presence with padding so nothing moves.

Before you keep reading — guess how many pixels of padding a 100-line copy-pasted "scroll lock" utility is usually off by, on the one OS nobody tested it on. The answer is almost always "enough to notice," because scrollbar width isn't a constant. It's roughly 17px on Windows across Chrome and Firefox alike, 0px on a Mac with overlay scrollbars — and the measurement has to run before you lock, every single time, or it reads the wrong number.

Why the shift happens at all

Here's the part the padding hack never actually fixes, it just hides: a classic scrollbar — the opaque kind with a visible track, standard on Windows and Linux — is laid out inside the element's content box. The browser treats it the same way it treats a sidebar: it eats width from whatever would otherwise render there. Turn the scrollbar off, and the content box grows back to full width. Turn it on, and the content box shrinks to make room. The content isn't "jumping" — it's being resized, every time, and resized fast enough that it reads as a flinch.

macOS's default overlay scrollbars don't do this. They float on top of the content without claiming any layout space, so toggling them on and off never changes anything's width. That's the whole reason this bug is invisible to a developer who only ever tests on their own Mac: the platform they build on structurally can't reproduce the thing their users are reporting.

The padding-right hack works around the resize by adding back exactly the width the scrollbar would have taken — but it only works if you already know the scrollbar is about to disappear, and you measured it correctly, before it does. It's compensating for a resize instead of preventing one.

scrollbar-gutter: stable: tell the layout to stop flinching

CSS has a property for exactly this now, and the name says what it does: reserve the scrollbar's gutter, stably, whether a scrollbar is currently needed or not.

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable;
}

Set this once, and the browser carves out the scrollbar's width in the layout permanently — for overflow: auto, scroll, and hidden. When your modal flips overflow to hidden to lock the page, the gutter is already reserved from before the modal ever opened. There's no width to give back, so there's nothing to resize, so there's nothing to flinch.

function lockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden"; // that's it — no measuring, no padding
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

That's the whole fix for the layout-shift half of what a scroll-lock library does. You still need something to stop the page actually scrolling under a modal on touch devices — overflow: hidden alone doesn't catch every edge case there, and that part of a scroll-lock library can stay. But the width-measuring, padding-compensating dance that most of these libraries built their reputation on? scrollbar-gutter: stable makes it dead code.

There's a second value for layouts that center content and need symmetry on both sides:

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable both-edges;
}

both-edges mirrors the reserved gutter to the opposite inline edge, so if space is held open on the right, matching space opens on the left too — useful when a scrollbar appearing on only one side would visibly knock a centered layout off-center.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that's easy to get wrong: overlay scrollbars opt out of this too

Here's the honest asterisk, and it's the same one from earlier in reverse: scrollbar-gutter: stable only reserves space for classic scrollbars. MDN says it plainly — "When using overlay scrollbars, the gutter will not be present." On a system with overlay scrollbars, setting this property changes nothing, because there was never any layout space being given up in the first place.

That means you can't fully verify this fix by eyeballing your own Mac. You need a Windows or Linux machine, a Windows/Linux VM, or Chrome DevTools' device toolbar won't help either — it emulates viewport size, not the host OS's scrollbar rendering mode. The honest test is someone, or something, running an actual classic-scrollbar environment.

Is this safe to ship today?

Yes, with one small caveat worth knowing rather than discovering. Chrome and Edge have supported scrollbar-gutter since version 94 (2021), and Firefox since version 97 (2022) — this has quietly worked for most of your users for years. Safari was the holdout; it landed support in Safari 18.2, released in December 2024, which is also what pushed scrollbar-gutter to Baseline "newly available" that same month. If you need to support Safari versions older than 18.2, the property is simply ignored there — no error, no warning, the page just behaves exactly like it always did. That's a safe degrade, not a broken one, so there's no reason to gate this behind a feature query unless you want to show a different UI specifically for browsers that lack it.

The next time a modal makes your page twitch, you'll know exactly why — and now you know the one-line reason to stop paying JavaScript to measure a number CSS can just reserve for you.

Still carrying a scroll-lock library in your bundle for this exact problem? Go check what it actually does under the hood — there's a decent chance half of it just became unnecessary.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.
