articles.title: Building an Image Compressor That Hits an Exact File Size
articles.description: Every upload form has the same annoying quirk: it rejects on file size, but every compressor gives...
articles.body_html:
Every upload form has the same annoying quirk: it rejects on file size, but every compressor gives you a quality slider instead of a size input.

So you end up in a loop. Compress, check size, compress again. Adjust quality from 80 to 70. Check again. 65. Again.

I wanted to invert that: give the tool the number, let it figure out the quality.

The problem with quality-first

JPEG file size doesn't vary linearly with the quality parameter. Going from q=0.9 to q=0.8 might drop the file by 40%, or by 8%, depending on the image content. That's why the manual loop feels so random.

But the relationship is monotonic — lower quality always means smaller file. That's enough for a binary search.

Binary search over quality

For a fixed image size, find the highest quality whose encoded blob is still under the target:

async function encodeUnderTarget(canvas, mime, targetBytes) {
  // Check the ceiling first: if even q=0.95 fits, done.
  const top = await toBlob(canvas, mime, 0.95);
  if (top.size <= targetBytes) return { blob: top, quality: 0.95 };

  let lo = 0.15, hi = 0.95, best = null;

  // 6 iterations narrows the range to ~1% — plenty for file size.
  for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    const blob = await toBlob(canvas, mime, mid);
    if (blob.size <= targetBytes) {
      best = { blob, quality: mid };
      lo = mid;          // this works, try higher quality
    } else {
      hi = mid;          // too big, try lower
    }
  }
  return best;           // null means even q=0.15 is too big
}

function toBlob(canvas, mime, quality) {
  return new Promise((resolve) =>
    canvas.toBlob((blob) => resolve(blob), mime, quality)
  );
}

Six encodes lands within a few percent below the target, instead of the 20-40% below you get from guessing a quality value.

When quality isn't enough

Some images can't hit the target at any quality — high-ISO photos, heavy noise, complex texture. So there's a second loop: if even q=0.15 overshoots, scale down and retry.

let scale = 1;
for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 6; attempt++) {
  const canvas = drawScaled(img, srcW * scale, srcH * scale);
  const result = await encodeUnderTarget(canvas, mime, targetBytes);
  if (result) return { ...result, scale };

  scale *= 0.7;   // 30% smaller each round
  if (Math.max(srcW, srcH) * scale < 48) break;
}

The 0.7 factor matters. At 0.9 you need many more rounds, and each round costs 6 encodes.

Three things that bit me

1. Transparent PNGs turn black in JPEG

canvas.toBlob(..., 'image/jpeg') composites onto black by default. You have to paint white first:

ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, w, h);
ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0, w, h);

2. Huge images make the search unusable

Each toBlob() on a 24MP canvas takes 300-500ms. Six encodes × six scale rounds = 30+ seconds. So downscale anything above ~12MP before searching:

const MAX_PIXELS = 12e6;
if (srcW * srcH > MAX_PIXELS) {
  scale = Math.sqrt(MAX_PIXELS / (srcW * srcH));
}

3. Files already under target shouldn't be re-encoded

If your 20KB file is already under 50KB, re-encoding it loses quality for zero benefit. Pass it through untouched:

if (file.size <= targetBytes) {
  return { blob: file, scale: 1, passthrough: true };
}

Results

Input Target Output Time
1600×1200 photo, 148 KB 50 KB 49 KB ~1.4s
3000×2000 photo, 2.7 MB 50 KB 50 KB ~7s
1200×900 photo, 88 KB 20 KB 20 KB ~0.7s
240×180, 14 KB 50 KB unchanged ~0.1s

What I'd like to know

  • Is binary search the right approach? libjpeg does something similar internally but I wanted pure JS with no wasm payload. Is there a smarter rate-control strategy?
  • WebP vs JPEG: WebP wins 25-35% at equal quality, and it's my default. But Safari's WebP encode path was historically slow — anyone have current numbers?
  • The 12MP cutoff: arbitrary. Below it, search feels instant; above it, it drags. Is there a better heuristic?

The tool is at imgpress-c90.pages.dev — no upload endpoint exists, you can go offline after the page loads and it still works. Source is plain JS, no build step.

articles.title: I built a free, offline photo resizer for Pakistani government forms (FPSC, PPSC, NADRA) — here's what the forms actually require
articles.description: Every government form in Pakistan has a different photo rule, and none of them explain it well: FPSC...
articles.body_html:
Every government form in Pakistan has a different photo rule, and none of them explain it well: FPSC wants a JPG under 30 KB, PPSC under 25 KB, Pak Navy under 20 KB, the passport portal 350x467 pixels. A phone photo is 3 MB. Thousands of applications fail at the upload step every week.

So I built FormKB (https://formkb.com), a set of browser-only tools: the photo never leaves the device (Canvas API, no upload), and each form has a preset read from the organisation's own guidelines PDF, quoted on the page.

A few things I learned building it:

  1. The limits on blogs are often wrong. I read the official documents and found PPSC's "140x177" and NTS's "50 KB" repeated everywhere without a source. Every preset on the site links the PDF it came from: https://formkb.com/photo-size-requirements

  2. "KB" is not a pixel size. People search "20 KB photo size in pixels" constantly, so I wrote the conversion down with a table instead of a formula that doesn't exist: https://formkb.com/guides/kb-to-pixels

  3. Binary search on JPEG quality beats guessing. The resizer picks the largest pixel size and quality that still fits under the limit, in the browser, usually in under a second.

  4. The same engine works for other countries' forms once you have the official spec: UK passport (600x750 px, 50 KB–10 MB), Bangladesh Teletalk (300x300 under 100 KB), India's JEE Main (10–200 KB): https://formkb.com/jee-main-photo-signature-size

Stack: Next.js static export on Cloudflare, no backend, no analytics. Tests run the real tools in headless Chrome against the stated limits (252 checks).

If you've fought a government upload form, I'd like to hear which one; the next presets come from those stories.

articles.title: From a 2017 Experiment to 800+ Commits: What Building Retro Paddle Taught Me
articles.description: It started with a simple question: could I still build a decent Pong-style game from scratch?  Back...
articles.body_html:
It started with a simple question: could I still build a decent Pong-style game from scratch?

Back in 2017 I opened a canvas and added two paddles, a ball and a score counter. It was a small experiment to see what I could make, and I put the result on YouTube: the first version from 2017.

In January 2024 I picked it up again. Almost two years, more than 800 commits and quite a few late evenings later, that experiment has grown into something much bigger. It now has more than 20 power-ups and power-downs, weapons, portals, sea mines, a computer opponent, online multiplayer and even its own dependency-free npm package.

I call it Retro Paddle, and you can play it right here:

Play Retro Paddle

It's free, needs no account or installation, and works on desktop and mobile. Below is how it grew, and a few things I learned along the way.

1. Plain JavaScript, paper and a set square

The very first version, in 2017, was plain JavaScript on an HTML canvas, without a framework, game engine or physics library. There were no AI coding tools to lean on back then either.

What I remember best from those early days is figuring out how the ball should bounce off the walls. I grabbed a piece of paper and a set square (a triangular ruler), drew the ball's incoming direction, marked the wall and worked out what the outgoing direction should look like. The angle of incidence had to equal the angle of reflection.

It might sound a little old-fashioned, but I really enjoyed working it out that way. I wanted to understand the maths and write the behaviour myself instead of pulling in a physics library, and that code is still the foundation of the game.

2. Turning Pong on its side

The next big decision was also one of the simplest: I didn't want another horizontal Pong game.

A horizontal field is fine on a desktop, but on a smartphone you either rotate your phone or squeeze the game into a narrow strip of screen. So I turned the whole thing 90 degrees.

In Retro Paddle the ball travels from top to bottom. You hold your phone upright, your paddle sits at the bottom, and the full height of the screen is your playing field. On a touchscreen you drag your finger anywhere and the paddle follows, so your thumb never covers the paddle you're trying to watch.

It sounds like a small change, but it shaped almost everything that came after: the layout, the controls, the gameplay and even how the power-ups work.

3. A name change I wish I'd made earlier

The npm package was originally called retro-pong-game.

Then I looked more closely at trademarks and found out that PONG is a registered trademark. I'd rather avoid trouble and give the project its own identity, so with version 7.0.0 everything became Retro Paddle.

The gameplay didn't change at all, but the package name, README, website, documentation and share images all needed updating. That was a surprisingly big job for something that didn't change a single pixel of the game!

If you're building your own take on a classic game, think about the name early. Picking a distinctive name at the start is much easier than changing it after you've built a whole project around it.

4. More than 20 power-ups, and one simple rule

Just hitting a ball back and forth gets repetitive after a while, so I started experimenting with power-ups and power-downs. There are now more than 20 of them, including:

  • Split Ball: suddenly you're dealing with multiple balls.
  • Gun: pick up a weapon and shoot at your opponent.
  • Portals: send the ball through a portal and change its path.
  • Safety Net: get another chance when a ball slips past your paddle.
  • Remote Steering: keep steering the ball after you hit it.
  • Mirror Paddle: a mirrored copy of your paddle guards the other side of the field.
  • Lag Spikes: make life a little more difficult for your opponent.
  • Phantom Balls: confuse your opponent with fake balls.

One design rule turned out to be really useful while building these: the ball is always moving away from you when an effect starts.

So anything that changes the ball reaches your opponent first. Collecting a Fast Ball is good news for you, because your opponent has less time to react. Collecting a Slow Ball actually helps your opponent.

Once I saw that, designing the colours, icons and visual feedback got much easier, because they could show who benefits from an item as well as what it does.

The core game is still the code I wrote myself, starting in 2017. For the power-ups and power-downs, which I added over the last two years, I used AI as a pair programmer. That made it much faster to try ideas, test different behaviours and keep the ones that made the game more fun. Not every idea made it in, of course. Some sounded great on paper and turned out to be incredibly annoying in an actual match!

5. Making the computer opponent feel human

A computer opponent that always wins isn't much fun, and neither is one that lets you win every match. I wanted something more dynamic without building a complicated AI system.

So the opponent reacts to scoring streaks. Score three times in a row and the computer starts trying harder. If the computer scores three in a row, it eases off a little.

It's a simple mechanic, but matches feel more balanced than with a fixed difficulty level. The computer can still be beaten, and both sides keep a fair chance of winning.

6. Online multiplayer without a traditional game server

Online multiplayer was probably the hardest part of the project. Getting two browsers to talk to each other was manageable. Keeping the game responsive once latency and packet loss came into play took a lot more work.

In the end I went for a fairly lightweight setup.

A Cloudflare Worker as a relay

The Worker knows nothing about the game and runs no gameplay logic. It just forwards messages between two connected browsers. Because the relay doesn't need to understand the messages, I can change the protocol as the game evolves without touching the server.

A loopback test page

This turned out to be one of my most useful tools. It's a separate page with two games running side by side, connected through a fake network where I can set the latency and packet loss.

That lets me simulate a bad connection whenever I want, without two computers or a real online connection. A network bug that might take a whole evening to reproduce in a real match can sometimes show up within seconds there.

My biggest takeaway from multiplayer: build your testing tools early. They save an enormous amount of time later.

7. It's also an npm package

At some point I realised the game could be useful outside my own website, so I moved the game itself into its own npm package.

You can embed Retro Paddle in an existing website without React, Vue or any other framework, and it has no external dependencies.

retro-paddle on npm

npm install retro-paddle

To get started, import the package and create a game:

import { PaddleGame } from 'retro-paddle';

const game = new PaddleGame({ isAdmin: true }, '#game');

The isAdmin option turns on a settings panel where you can adjust colours, sizes, speeds and other settings live. When you're happy with the result, you copy the settings as JSON and reuse them.

I deliberately kept online multiplayer out of the package. The network code only lives on my website, so nobody who embeds the game gets networking code they never asked for.

You can try the package and read the setup instructions on the demo page:

Retro Paddle demo and setup

8. Years later, and I'm still adding things

Looking back, I'm surprised by how much this project has grown. A small canvas experiment from 2017 became a game with its own mechanics, an online mode, a computer opponent and a reusable npm package.

Along the way I've learned a lot about game development, structuring JavaScript, networking and testing, and about how much small helper tools speed up development.

Maybe the biggest lesson is that you don't need a big idea to start building something interesting. A ball, two paddles and some curiosity can be enough. And a couple of evenings, although in my case it turned out to be quite a few more than that!

Give Retro Paddle a try!

If you've made it this far, I'd love for you to give it a go:

Play Retro Paddle

You can play the computer, challenge someone on the same keyboard, or invite a friend to an online match. It's free, there's no signup and it works on your phone too.

Here's a video of Retro Paddle in action:

Watch Retro Paddle on YouTube

I'm especially curious about a few things:

  • Which power-up do you think is the most unfair?
  • How does the game feel on your phone?
  • Do you have ideas for power-ups or features that would make it even more fun?

And if you've built a browser game yourself, drop a link in the comments. I'd love to check it out!

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Why We Ditched a 30MB AI Model and Built a <2.5ms Canvas Snapper in TypeScript
articles.description: How we replaced a 30MB Segment-Anything model with 200 lines of classical TypeScript, achieving <2.5ms canvas element-snapping with zero dependencies.
articles.body_html:
When building FocusFlow — a spatial storytelling canvas that turns architecture diagrams into 60fps cinematic presentations — we faced an intriguing computer vision problem: Click-to-Snap.

When a user imports a rasterized architecture diagram (PNG/JPEG/SVG) and clicks anywhere inside an element (like an ECS task card, a VPC boundary, or a database cylinder), the engine needs to extract its precise bounding box in < 5ms to smoothly anchor camera viewport frustums.

1. The Initial Mirage: WebGPU + MobileSAM

In 2026, the knee-jerk reaction for image segmentation in the browser is to reach for a machine learning model:

  • Run a quantized Segment Anything (MobileSAM) model via ONNX Runtime Web.
  • Offload inference to WebGPU.

The Real-World Costs:

  • Payload Penalty: An initial ~30MB model download.
  • VRAM Overhead: 250MB–350MB GPU buffer allocation.
  • Latency Friction: 120ms–180ms inference per click.
  • Failure Modes: Over-segmenting internal text lines or bleeding into complex canvas backgrounds.

For a lightweight web application that users open in their desktop browser, forcing a 30MB weight download just to detect rectangles felt like engineering malpractice.

We asked ourselves: Can classical computer vision, implemented in pure TypeScript and tuned for CSS geometry, beat neural nets in speed, accuracy, and footprint?

2. Five Real-World CSS Edge Cases That Break Naive Sobel

Traditional Sobel gradient filters assume simple solid shapes on clean contrast. But modern UI diagrams look nothing like that:

  1. Text Hole Perforation: Cards are packed with bold headers, monospace code snippets, and badge pills. High-frequency font glyph edges easily trick naive ray-casters into snapping to inner text.
  2. CSS Linear Gradients: Backgrounds subtly drift across 400px. Standard global thresholding either cuts off mid-card or bleeds across boundaries.
  3. Emoji & Colorful Badges: Clicking directly on an inline icon (e.g. 🛡️ or 🐘) corrupts single-point background color sampling.
  4. Long Title Blockades: A 24-character monospace title forms a contiguous horizontal boundary that cuts the card's flood-fill front in half.
  5. Dark-on-Dark Contrast: Dark-mode cards (#0f172a) against canvas backgrounds (#0c1220) yield miniscule perceptual color differences ($\Delta E < 25$) surrounded by diffuse drop shadows.

3. The Pure Math Architecture: A 3-Tier Pipeline

To solve this without machine learning, we built a 3-tier deterministic pipeline:

3.1 Compact 3-Ring Profiler (Phase 1.6)

Instead of single-point sampling, we sample 33 concentric points across 4 rings ($r \in [1, 8, 16, 24]\text{px}$). Each sample is weighted inversely by its local Sobel gradient flatness:
$$W_i = \max(1, 35 - G_i)$$
High-gradient text pixels are suppressed, while flat card pixels dominate. If a cluster fails validation, a Top-3 candidate fallback loop recovers the true background.

3.2 Floating Gradient BFS

Rather than comparing against an absolute seed color, our BFS tracks local step-to-step color deviation ($\Delta E_{\text{step}} \le 8$).

  • On flat background pixels, expensive $3 \times 3$ Sobel convolution is bypassed entirely.
  • This optimization dropped BFS runtime from 106ms down to 1.8ms (a 58x speedup).

3.3 Spatially Separable Anisotropic Morphological Closing

To seal text perforations without blurring vertical card edges, we employ an anisotropic separable kernel:

  • Horizontal kernel ($r_x = 6\text{px}$): Locks tight around card borders.
  • Vertical kernel ($r_y = 14\text{px}$): Bridges across multi-line text lines and headers. Because the 2D kernel is mathematically separable into 1D passes, algorithmic complexity drops from $O(K^2)$ to $O(2K)$, saving 90% of active pixel computations.

4. Memory & Zero-GC Guarantees

JavaScript garbage collection pauses are the enemy of smooth 60fps canvas interaction.

  • All intermediate masks and flood-fill queues utilize pre-allocated Uint8Array and Float32Array pools.
  • Total heap footprint is strictly capped under 450 KB.
  • Result: 0 GC collections during click-and-drag interactions.

5. Benchmarks & Industrial Validation

Across our 20-suite automated E2E test matrix (including nested cloud diagrams, dark-mode wireframes, and accent-bar cards):

  • End-to-End Latency: < 2.5ms
  • TypedArray Memory: < 450 KB
  • External Dependencies: 0 KB
  • Pass Rate: 20 / 20 PASS (100%)

Conclusion

Sometimes the most scalable engineering decision in 2026 is not to deploy a transformer model. For structured UI domains, classical computer vision combined with modern TypedArrays delivers 60x faster performance with zero bundle bloat.

Our full architecture and implementation details are open-sourced:

  • Repository: https://github.com/tumio-ltd/focusflow
  • Live Demo: https://focusflow.tumio.site

articles.title: Your logos folder is already out of date
articles.description: Copying brand SVGs into /public/logos feels free until a brand changes its logo. Here is why a versioned icon library beats hosting your own files, with a five minute setup.
articles.body_html:
Open your project and look for a folder named logos, brands or partners. It probably holds a couple of dozen SVGs you downloaded one at a time, with names like github-new.svg, stripe-2021.svg and slack_final_v2.svg.

That folder was correct on the day you made it. It has been drifting ever since, and nothing in your build will tell you.

I learned this the hard way. Our template catalog showed a logo for 63 of 442 apps, because someone copied 63 files by hand and nobody wanted to copy the rest. The other 379 tiles showed a gray letter. The marks existed. They just lived somewhere else.

What goes wrong with hosted logo files

Copying a file gives you a snapshot. Brands do not stand still, and a snapshot has four ways to go bad.

  • The brand changes its logo, and your site keeps showing the old one.
  • The file was never clean. It has a hard-coded size, no viewBox, a script tag, or a "mono" version that secretly uses four colors.
  • Each file is a one-off, so no two have the same name, the same dark mode story or the same license note.
  • Nobody owns it. A designer drops a file in, a developer renames it, and nobody can say where it came from.

A hosted folder also costs you bytes you cannot see. A sprite sheet of every logo you might need loads on the page that needs only one.

The fix: treat logos like a dependency

You already treat React, your date library and your CSS framework this way. Somebody else maintains them, you pin a version, and you upgrade on purpose. Brand logos can work the same way.

theSVG is an open catalog of more than 7,600 brand icons with a rule that every icon follows the same path scheme: {slug}/{variant}.svg. The GitHub logo is always github. Its dark version is always github/dark.svg. When the brand changes the mark, the new one lands under the same name.

That one rule is what makes updates automatic.

Seven reasons a library beats your own folder

The first reason is the one that matters most. The other six are what keep it that way.

Reason What it means for you
Same name, new icon A rebrand ships in a version bump, with no code change
One naming scheme default, mono, light, dark and wordmark everywhere
Checked in CI No scripts, no raster data, a real viewBox, mono files that are truly single color
Rebrands keep history The old mark stays as a -legacy entry, so nothing vanishes
Tree-shaking Import one icon and ship one icon
License on every entry You can see the rules before you ship
Signed releases npm packages publish with provenance

The checks are not decoration. Last week we added 27 new self-hosted app icons to theSVG, and the validator rejected our first pull request. Six files carried editor metadata, and one "mono" variant was not single color. The bad files never reached a release.

How to check how stale your folder is

You can find out in ten minutes. List every file in the folder and ask three questions about each one.

First, where did it come from? If the answer is "a Google image search," treat it as untrusted. Second, does it open cleanly? Run it through an SVG linter and look for a missing viewBox, a fixed width and height, or embedded PNG data. Third, is it still the brand's current mark? Open the company's own site next to your copy and compare.

Most folders fail at least one of those checks. The failures are rarely dramatic. A slightly different blue, a retired gradient, a wordmark with the old typeface. Visitors rarely notice any single one, but together they make a page look less cared for.

Setup in five minutes

Pick the line that matches your stack.

# React
npm install @thesvg/react

# Astro
npm install @thesvg/astro

# Plain JavaScript, tree-shakeable
npm install thesvg

# No install, copy one icon into your repo
npx @thesvg/cli add github

Then use an icon the way you use any component. The variant prop picks the light, dark, mono or wordmark version, so dark mode is one prop instead of a second file.

import Github from "@thesvg/react/github";

export function Footer() {
  return <Github width={24} height={24} variant="dark" aria-label="GitHub" />;
}

In Astro, the import path is the same idea.

---
import Github from "@thesvg/astro/github";
---
<Github size={24} />

If you only need an image tag, the CDN works with no install at all.

<img src="https://thesvg.org/icons/github/default.svg" width="32" height="32" alt="GitHub" />

Let your tools do the updating

The real payoff is the part you stop doing. Add the package to Dependabot or Renovate and a new icon version arrives as a normal pull request. Your logos improve while you work on something else.

We did this on our own product. The dashboard used a hand-kept list that matched each of 442 app templates to a logo file. We replaced it with a small script that reads the template ids, checks which marks exist in the installed package and writes the mapping. Now a version bump of @thesvg/react is the whole job. Version 4.0.3 added 27 icons, which unlocked 34 more tiles without adding a single file.

What about brands that are not there yet

Tell us, or add them yourself. Every icon starts as a pull request with the SVG and a small data entry, and the same checks run on yours. If a project is real, it belongs in the catalog. The library is open source under the MIT license, with no accounts and no API keys.

You can also ask your AI editor. The @thesvg/mcp-server package lets your AI editor look up and insert logos for you, so you never have to leave the file you are editing.

Try it on one file

Do not migrate everything today. Pick one component that imports a logo from your logos folder, swap it for the library version, and delete the file. If you like the result, do the next one.

If theSVG saves you a trip to a press kit, a star on GitHub is the best way to help other developers find it.

glincker / thesvg

The open SVG brand library: 7,600+ brand logos and cloud icons (AWS, Azure, GCP) as official SVG. Search, copy, ship via npm, CDN, CLI, React, Vue, Svelte, Figma, VS Code, Raycast and MCP. Free, MIT, no gatekeeping.

The open SVG brand library

A HOME FOR EVERY BRAND.

7,600+ brand logos and cloud icons. Search, copy and ship them as SVG, React, Vue, Svelte, CDN, CLI or MCP.
Free, open source, no gatekeeping

Browse icons  •  Quick start  •  Install  •  Extensions  •  CDN  •  API  •  Packages  •  Compare  •  Community  •  Contribute  •  Contributors

Every logo below is served straight from theSVG.

                                   

                                   

Why theSVG

Brand logos are scattered across press kits, Figma files, and random GitHub repos. theSVG is the single source for SVG icons - brand logos, cloud architecture diagrams, and a set of interface icons of our own. Searchable, versioned, and available as npm packages, CDN, CLI, API, and MCP server.

Every developer has hunted for a company logo: a press kit buried three clicks deep, a PNG that blurs on retina, a "mono" file that is secretly four colors, a logo that changed…

articles.title: Your API Errors Shouldn't Be a Guessing Game
articles.description: Imagine you're building a frontend application and an API request fails.  The backend returns:    {  ...
articles.body_html:
Imagine you're building a frontend application and an API request fails.

The backend returns:

{
  "message": "Something went wrong"
}

Great. But what went wrong?

Was it a validation error? A missing resource? A permission issue? Or something else?

Now the frontend has to guess what happened.

There's a better way to handle API errors, and it's already standardized.

The Problem With API Errors

Different APIs often return errors in different formats.

One endpoint returns:

{
  "error": "Invalid email"
}

Another returns:

{
  "message": "User not found",
  "code": 404
}

And another might accidentally expose an internal database error.

This makes frontend development harder because every endpoint needs different error-handling logic.

What if every API followed the same error structure?

Meet Problem Details

RFC 7807 introduced a standard format called Problem Details for HTTP APIs.

It was later replaced by RFC 9457, which is the current standard.

The idea is simple: return errors in a consistent, predictable format.

Here's an example:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient Funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Your balance is $40, but the total is $55.",
  "instance": "/checkouts/123"
}

Much better, right?

Every field has a purpose:

  • type: Identifies the kind of error.
  • title: A short description of the problem.
  • status: The HTTP status code.
  • detail: Explains what happened in this request.
  • instance: Identifies the specific occurrence of the problem.

The API should also return the appropriate HTTP status code and this content type:

Content-Type: application/problem+json

Now the frontend knows what kind of problem occurred without guessing from random messages.

What About Form Validation?

This is where it gets even more useful.

Imagine a registration form with invalid inputs.

Your API could return:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 422,
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "Invalid email address"
    },
    {
      "field": "password",
      "message": "Must contain at least 8 characters"
    }
  ]
}

The errors array is a custom extension, not a required field in the standard.

Now the frontend can display each error beside the correct input.

No need to parse random error strings.

Handling Errors in JavaScript

Here's a simple example using fetch:

const response = await fetch("/api/register", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(formData)
});

if (!response.ok) {
  const problem = await response.json();

  if (problem.type === "https://api.example.com/problems/validation") {
    console.log(problem.errors);
  } else {
    console.error(problem.title);
  }
}

In a real application, you should also handle network failures and responses that don't contain valid JSON.

The important part is that your frontend can rely on documented error types instead of matching message strings.

A Few Things Worth Remembering

Using Problem Details doesn't automatically solve every error-handling problem.

You still need to follow a few good practices:

  • Never expose stack traces, SQL queries, or internal secrets.
  • Keep error types stable so frontend code doesn't break.
  • Use appropriate HTTP status codes.
  • Use safe, user-friendly messages where appropriate.
  • Add a request ID when useful for debugging and support.

For localization, frontend applications can map stable error types to translated messages instead of relying on English error descriptions.

Final Thoughts

A good API isn't just about returning successful responses.

It's also about explaining failures clearly.

RFC 9457 gives us a standard way to do that.

No random error structures. No guessing from message strings. Just predictable errors that both frontend and backend developers can understand.

And the best part?

You don't need a new library or framework to get started. Just a consistent error format.

How are you currently handling API errors in your projects?
